post.summary: Start a program or port instance
post.description:
Starts the program immediately. For port-range programs, the "port" parameter is required to specify which instance to start. Optional "wait" parameter blocks until the program is running (with `ready_port`, until it serves). Optional "if_not_running" parameter makes the operation idempotent (safe to call multiple times). Use if_not_running for edge proxy automation. Program must be enabled. The body is REQUIRED: a request with no body, or without `Content-Type: application/json`, is refused as a 400 carrying the `{success: false, error}` envelope; so is a body that is not JSON or has a field of the wrong type (`invalid request body: ...`). Send `{}` when every field is defaulted.

**Response.** A standard program answers `{"success": true}` (plus `already_running` with `if_not_running`); only a port-range start carries `instance`. Without `wait`, success does not confirm that the program reached the running state: use `wait` or query status to confirm. A confirmed start failure is a 400 whose `error` says why; when it was the first attempt that failed, the program may still be retried and come up, so check its status. 

**`wait`.** With `wait: true` the call polls until the program is reported running and, when it declares `ready_port`, until the program accepts the TCP connection the daemon opens to that port from inside the computer. A `ready_port` program is ready while still starting once only its own processes listen on that port; a program that crashes before it listens is still a failed start. A program that never accepts connections there stays unready and the call times out. A program that finishes during the wait answers 200 with `status: "exited"` and its `last_run`, whatever the exit code; a start that ends in `fatal`, or that was refused, is a 400 that carries `last_run`. A finished run never counts as ready: a caller that needs the program to serve (`ready_port`, `if_not_running`) gets a 400 saying it exited before accepting connections. `timeout` is the readiness polling budget in seconds (0 to 4294967295, default 30). Configuration and the start itself happen before it begins, so the request can take longer; `0` ends a newly entered wait at once as a timeout. With `if_not_running`, an already-running or shared result can come back instead, and the already-running shortcut for a port-range instance does not check `ready_port`. Set a client-side HTTP timeout longer than the budget. 

**`if_not_running`.** Concurrent idempotent starts for the same id and port share one start, whatever their own `wait` and `timeout`: a waiting caller can receive an earlier non-waiting caller's `starting`. After it finished, only a WAITED result that found the program ready is reused, for about 2 seconds, and only while that run is observably alive and has not reported an end. Anything else (a start nobody waited for, a failed or finished result, a run the daemon cannot observe) is not reused; the next caller checks again and starts the program if it is not running. A caller whose wait for a shared start runs out gets a 400 (`start is still in progress ... retry`) and no second start. Poll status when confirmation matters. 

**Sandboxed programs.** A launch the sandbox refuses for its configuration exits 78 (`EX_CONFIG`) with one `sandbox: <reason>` line on stderr; a launch cancelled by a stop signal, or whose sandbox setup failed, exits 143 unless a sandbox setup step already exited with its own nonzero status, which is passed through; a signal death is `128+n`. Status shows the state (typically `fatal`) and can include `last_run` with the exit code or launch error; the program's stderr log has the full reason.

post.summary: Restart a program or port instance
post.description:
Stops, then starts again, the program (or the chosen instances of a port-range program) in one call, and answers a receipt. Done is `state: completed` with `outcome: restarted`: every targeted process runs under a new process id, given in `instances`.

A stop the process manager did not confirm starts nothing; it and a start whose reply was lost or whose wait ran out answer 502 with `state: unknown`: the program may or may not be running, so read it again (`GET /programs/overview`, or this receipt by its key) before acting. Nothing is retried.

The program is read again, and a held key looked up again, once the restart has the program's turn: a program disabled or edited meanwhile is refused or restarted as it now stands. The restart finishes even if the caller goes away. Errors carry a `code` and a fixed sentence; the reason, which can quote the program's command, is only in the daemon log.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: 1 to 255 printable ASCII characters. After the request passes validation the daemon holds the key, bound to this program and body, before it restarts anything. The same key with the same program and body answers the receipt as it stands (200) and never restarts again, while the program exists; the same key with another program or body is refused (422). post.description:
Creates and starts a temporary custom program. Custom programs only: system services (`apache2`, `nginx`, etc.) belong under `systemctl`.

**Key features:**
- Not saved with permanent programs (temporary only); tracked separately with its result, so it survives a daemon restart
- Never started automatically on reboot
- Lifetime: an optional `ttl` bounds the whole execution from launch, across retries and restarts; `expires_at` is that deadline. When it passes the program is stopped and `last_run.error` reads `ttl expired` (checked every 10 seconds, so not exact).
- Results: once the program finishes (`exited` with no restart to follow, `fatal`, or stopped through the stop endpoint) its definition is withdrawn and its status, `last_run` and logs stay readable for 10 minutes; then status and logs answer 404. Log files are never deleted.
- Daemon restart: a program that finished while the daemon was down keeps its recorded exit code; one still running is stopped and its `last_run.error` reads `daemon restarted before the program finished`.
- The returned `temporary_id` has the form `quick_<milliseconds>_<sequence>`; it is not a numeric program id. Every response after creation carries it, errors included.
- `wait: true` returns when the command finishes (200, `status: "exited"` and `last_run`, whatever the exit code) or when a long-running program is running. A wait that times out does not cancel the launch. A start whose reply was lost answers 502 and is never retried.
- Runs once by default: `autorestart` defaults to `"false"` here (persistent programs default to `"unexpected"`), so a failing command is not run again. Set `autorestart` to have it restarted.
- The same `autorestart`, `environment` and log settings as permanent programs

**Suited to:**
- One-off data migrations with custom scripts
- Temporary test servers for your applications
- Debug / development tasks
- CI/CD ephemeral environments
- Custom batch jobs

**Use for:** `python my_migration.py`, `node test-server.js`, `./my-batch-job.sh`
**Don't use for:** system services like `apache2`, `nginx`, `postgresql`. Use `systemctl`.

Use `POST /programs/add` for permanent custom programs that must survive reboots.

**No sandbox. A non-null `sandbox` value is refused with 400; `null` is accepted as absent. Ephemeral programs are not sandboxable in this revision; use `POST /programs/add` for a confined program. A top-level key that looks like a misspelt `sandbox` (`sandbx`, `Sandbox`, `sand_box`) is refused with 400 too, instead of being ignored like other unknown keys.

Every error after the program was created carries its `temporary_id`, and `last_run` when a result is known (a start that was refused or given up on, or a definition that did not load, whose status then reads `failed`). A body that is not JSON, lacks a required field or has a field of the wrong type is refused before the program is created, as `invalid request body: <reason>`; a request without `Content-Type: application/json` is a 400 as well.

get.description:
Live tail of a program's stdout or stderr log over Server-Sent Events: first the last `lines` complete lines, then every line appended afterwards, until the client disconnects. Program, `type` and `port` select the file exactly as in `GET /api/v1/daemon/programs/{id}/logs`, and the same requests are refused with the same JSON 400s before the stream starts. The file is re-examined four times a second.

Events (each `data:` is one JSON object, described by the 200 schema):
- `open` (first, once the file is open or known to be missing): `log_file`, `type`, `offset` (where following starts) and `exists`. A log file that does not exist yet is not an error: the stream waits for it.
- `line` (one complete line without its line terminator): `line`, `offset`. The SSE `id` equals `offset`, the byte position just past the line, so a reconnect with `Last-Event-ID` (or `offset`) continues with the next line. Invalid UTF-8 is replaced with U+FFFD rather than refused, and a line longer than 64 KiB arrives in pieces.
- `reset`: `reason` `rotated` (a new file now sits at the path; the old file is read to its end first) or `truncated` (the file shrank in place); reading restarts at offset 0.
- `error`: the stream cannot continue (for example the path now resolves outside the log directory); `error`. The server closes the stream after it. If the file exists but cannot be opened or read when the stream starts, the stream sends `error` instead of `open` and closes.
- `: keepalive` comment lines while the log is quiet (every 15 s).

At most 32 log streams are open across the daemon at once; the next is a 429.

parameters.description: Log stream: stdout or stderr

parameters.name: lines
parameters.description: Number of complete lines replayed from the end of the file before following (default 100). `0` replays nothing and only follows; values above 10000 are clamped to 10000. The replay is found in the last 10 MiB of the file. Ignored when resuming with `offset` or `Last-Event-ID`.

parameters.name: port
parameters.description: Port number (required for port-range programs)

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Resume cursor: the `id` of the last `line` event received (a byte offset just past that line). Streaming restarts at the next line and no backlog is replayed. An offset beyond the end of the current file means it was truncated or replaced since: the stream sends a `reset` event and starts from the top of the file. The cursor is a byte position, not a file identity, so a file replaced by one at least as long is not detected across a reconnect. Takes precedence over `Last-Event-ID`.

A malformed `lines` value is refused as plain text. Every JSON refusal here carries only `success` and `error`. A file that exists but cannot be opened or read after the stream is accepted is reported as an SSE `error` event, after which the stream closes.

post.description:
Stops the program, records its result and withdraws its definition. The entry is KEPT: its status, `last_run` and logs stay readable for 10 minutes after it finished, and its log files are never deleted.

**Actions performed:**
1. Stop the program (a stop that is not confirmed is logged and does not end the request)
2. Record the result with `status: "stopped"`: the run's own report when there is one, otherwise the process manager's record
3. Withdraw the program's definition

**Result:** `cleaned_up: true` means the withdrawal was CONFIRMED: the program's definition is gone. `cleaned_up: false` means the result is recorded but the withdrawal is still owed; the entry remembers that, and the daemon retries it in the background and at its next start before the entry is ever dropped. Either way the answer is 200. Once the withdrawal is confirmed the program cannot start again; while it is still owed and the stop itself was not confirmed, the program may still be restarted under its `autorestart` policy until a retry completes the withdrawal.

Stopping a program that already finished changes nothing about its result and answers 200 (completing a withdrawal that was still owed); an id that is unknown, or whose retention has ended, is a 404.

get.description:
Captures a fresh screenshot of the display and returns the image file.

The image spans the whole screen at its current size, read from the
windows as they are at the time of the call: pixel (x, y) is screen
point (x, y), the point `POST /input/click-at` with that `x` and `y`
clicks. Where no window is, the image is transparent. With `region`,
the image is that part of the screen and starts at its `x1,y1`.

A display with no window at all is not an error: the capture is a
screen-sized PNG that is transparent throughout, described and stored
in the history like any other capture.

**Response Formats:**
- Binary PNG image (default)
- Base64 JSON (with `?base64=true`): `info` describes the stored capture and `image`
  carries the picture. With `region`, `info` still describes the full image and the
  cropped `image` has no `dataUrl`. With `cursor`, the answer also has the pointer
  position as `cursor`.

**Known Failure Mode:**
Returns `SCREENSHOT_FAILED` when no image could be captured (for example, the display's windows could not be read in time).

With `cursor`, the pointer is read in the display's input queue: a full queue is a 429
`QUEUE_FULL`.

Starts a display that is waiting for its first use (the first start can take up to about 10
seconds), after the request has been checked: a request refused with a 400 leaves the display
waiting, except a `region` outside the screen, which only the capture can tell.

parameters.description:
Return base64-encoded JSON response instead of binary image.
Useful for AI agents and systems that can't handle binary data.

Accepted values:
- `true`, `1`, `` (empty) - Return base64 JSON
- `false`, `0` - Return binary (default)

parameters.name: displayId
parameters.description:
Display ID to use (overrides the `*-display-N.*` hostname pattern).

Crop the returned image to `x1,y1,x2,y2`. Minimum 10x10 px, maximum
65535 on each axis, `x2 > x1` and `y2 > y1`; anything else, an empty
`region` or one given twice included, is a 400.

A capture spans the whole screen, so these are screen coordinates: the
same ones `POST /input/click-at` takes and
`GET /input/display-geometry` describes. The cropped image starts at
`x1,y1`: its pixel (x, y) is screen point (x1 + x, y1 + y).

The region must lie inside the captured screen (`x2` at most its width,
`y2` at most its height): one that does not is a 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR`
naming the screen size. That check needs the capture, so it comes after
the display was started.

Include the pointer position in the response. Only has an effect on the
base64 JSON form, which gains a `cursor` object; a binary PNG response
has nowhere to put it.

Accepted values: `true`, `1`, `` (empty). Anything else is off.

  the form without dashes are not accepted. A date first matches the screenshot whose

  file was written, which can be a few seconds after `timestamp`, so one second can name two
  different screenshots. Unix time matches `timestamp` only.

  (`1749541160.4242.17.png`), or the whole path, URL-encoded. This names exactly that

`window`. Characters that the display's keyboard layout lacks
(accented letters, symbols, CJK) are added to the layout before
typing and stay there, so they are typed like any other key. Without

units.

(`\t`) presses Tab. For any other key or a combination (Escape,
ctrl+l, arrow keys), use `POST /api/v1/display/keyboard/key`.

post.summary: Execute one action with optional screenshot
post.description:
Runs one action, then (unless `screenshot` is false) waits `screenshotDelay` and takes a
screenshot. The action runs first, so if the screenshot or its crop then fails, the input
was delivered all the same: the answer is an error that says so in `details.message` and
carries the action's own answer in `action`, as a success would. Its code is the failure's
own (`SCREENSHOT_FAILED` with a 500; `DISPLAY_NOT_AVAILABLE` with a 503; a 400
`VALIDATION_ERROR` for a crop outside the image), never `INPUT_ACTION_FAILED`, which
means the action itself failed. Do not retry the action for such an answer: take a
screenshot instead. A caller that disconnects before the screenshot gets none taken.

`action` and `params` are the same as for one entry of `/input/batch`; the answer carries
what the action read back in `action.result` (see the batch result). A bad action or bad
`params` is a 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR`, answered before anything runs, and so is an invalid
`screenshotRegion`. The screenshot is the base64 form of `GET /screenshot`, and
`screenshot.timestamp` is its Unix timestamp in seconds.

Starts a display that is waiting for its first use (the first start can take up to about 10
seconds), after the request has been checked: a request refused by those checks (a body
or parameter error, or a `window/search` pattern the pre-start check finds has a syntax
error) leaves the display waiting. Once the request passes them it starts the display,
even when the action is `input/wait` and `screenshot` is false. A check that needs the
running display, such as an `input/click-at` point outside the display, can still answer
400 after the display has started.

post.description:
Runs the actions in order, as ordinary entries in the per-display input
queue, and stops at the first one that fails. The entries are queued one at a
time, so input of other requests to the same display can run between two of
your actions: a batch is ordered, but it is not atomic. Clipboard entries
are queue entries like the others; only an `input/wait` entry runs outside
the queue.

**A failing action is still HTTP 200.** Only the envelope can be
rejected (a missing or oversized `actions` array, or no display
context): once the request itself is valid, every per-action outcome
(a bad `params`, a full queue, a window that is gone, a display that
stopped answering) is reported in the body as `success: false` with
`failed: {index, action, error}` and `skipped`. Clients that branch on
the status code alone will read a failed batch as a success.

The aggregate budget is 60 s. It is checked before each action starts
and again when the action reaches the front of the queue, so an entry
that spent the budget waiting behind other requests is refused rather
than delivered late. It is not a hard limit on the response time: an
action that is already running finishes within its own timeout, so the
request can take longer than 60 s. Two answers mean the budget ran out. When it is
spent before an action starts, `failed.error` is "Batch timeout exceeded". When it is
spent while an action waits its turn in the queue, `failed.error` is "Command deadline
passed while it waited in the queue". An action that was already running when the budget
ended is not turned into a failure by the elapsed time alone: if it finishes, it is
reported as completed, and a final action that does so ends the batch with
`success: true`. An `input/wait` that would end after the budget is not cut short: it
fails at once with "Batch timeout exceeded: the wait would end after the batch budget",
and the actions after it are skipped. A nested `input/wait` takes `ms` only;
`screenshot: true` there is a failed entry (use `/input/act` for a screenshot).

`skipped` lists the actions that were not run, and is left out when
there are none.

A display that is waiting for its first use is started (the first start can take up to
about 10 seconds) only when an action before the first invalid entry acts on the display,
that is, is anything other than `input/wait`. A batch made only of `input/wait` entries,
or one whose first entry is invalid, leaves the display waiting. A `window/search` entry
whose pattern does not compile is a failed entry; the display is not started for it when
the pre-start check detects the syntax error. If that check is unavailable, times out or
hits a resource limit, the display can start before the entry fails.

If the client disconnects mid-batch, the action already running is
allowed to finish (interrupting a half-delivered key sequence is worse),
an `input/wait` ends at once, and nothing after it is dispatched: on a shared display, input nobody is
waiting for would otherwise land on whatever the next user is doing.

post.summary: Wait for a window to appear or disappear
post.description:
Blocks until the condition holds or the timeout expires, so a caller
does not have to poll `window/search` over HTTP while an application
starts up or a dialog closes.

A condition that stayed false for the whole timeout is **200** with
`timedOut: true`, not an error: it is control flow, the same choice
`/input/batch` makes for a failed entry. Errors keep the ordinary
contract, so "we could not observe the display" is never reported as
"the condition was false".

The poll runs outside the per-display input queue, so waiting never
occupies a queue slot, never delays a timed key or button release, and
never answers 429 because of queued input. It has its own admission
cap instead: 4 concurrent waits per display and 16 per process, over
which it answers 429 `QUEUE_FULL`.

`timeoutMs` is capped at 25000 on purpose: the generated SDK's
transport timeout defaults to 30 s, so a longer server budget would
abort in the client before the `timedOut` body could be read.

Starts a display that is waiting for its first use (the first start can take up to about 10
seconds), after the request has been checked: a body that fails validation or a request
refused with 429 leaves the display waiting, and so does a pattern whose syntax error the
pre-start check detects. If that check is unavailable, times out or hits a resource limit,
the display can start before the pattern is refused.

The server's storage check did not pass (for example, the mount directory and the directory of the backends' own mounts overlap), so no mount or backend connection can start, and backend file operations are refused. When the check fails on the service's own directories, the message goes on to name the directory (the state or the run directory), what is wrong with it (for example, a directory above it that is writable by group or others, or owned by another user) and how to correct it. post.description: Execute a script with POST data. Every HTTP method reaches the same script route, but behavior can depend on the method: a script that exports method-specific handlers runs the matching one, and HEAD falls back to GET. If no matching or catch-all handler exists, OPTIONS returns 204 and other methods return 405, with an Allow header. Other exceptions: OPTIONS is answered 204 by the CORS preflight before any script runs, unless a proxy hook dispatches it. A HEAD request runs the script but sends no body. PUT, PATCH and DELETE read a request body as POST does, and so does every other method except GET and HEAD when the request carries one (a Content-Length above 0 or a Transfer-Encoding), parsed by its Content-Type (JSON, form, multipart or raw bytes) unless the script declares `@rawBody`. A path ending in `.md` returns that documentation file instead of running a script, with or without a script beside it; beside a script it is served under that script's `@enabled` and `@token`. `/favicon.ico` is answered by the service itself (on an exclusive execId origin, one whose deployment directory holds an `.exclusive` marker, only that directory's own `favicon.ico` is served, else 404). When a proxy hook on this URL dispatches the request, OPTIONS, `.md` and `/favicon.ico` requests reach the hook script too, and it answers: `metadata.hook.forward()` relays the upstream's response; when the upstream cannot be reached, the hook script's `onUpstreamError` fallback answers, or the service answers 502 without a usable one. The hook's deadline answers 504, or closes the connection when the answer had already started. The script can answer with any status, Content-Type and body of its own; the statuses listed are the ones the service itself sends or falls back to.

200.description: The script's answer, or a documentation file. A script can set any status with `res.status()` and a Content-Type with `res.setHeader()`; without them the defaults below apply. A Content-Type the script set is kept for a returned object (other than an `Error`), string, stream (an async generator or `ReadableStream`) or other value; a returned `Response`'s own or detected Content-Type replaces it. A returned Buffer gets the type detected from its bytes, and a returned stream without a Content-Type gets `text/plain`. Headers the script already sent (`res.stream()`, `res.writeHead()`) stand. An object or array is sent as JSON. A string that starts, after leading whitespace, with `<!doctype html`, an HTML comment or an opening tag of a standard HTML element (`<h1>`, `<div class="x">`, `<svg>`) is sent as HTML. Any other string or value is sent as plain text, and a returned stream or async generator is written as it produces. A Buffer is sent with the type detected from its bytes. A returned `Response` is forwarded with its own status and headers, less the framing and hop-by-hop ones; one the script built without a Content-Type gets one from its first chunk when that chunk decodes as UTF-8: `application/json` when it starts as JSON, `text/html` when it starts as HTML (the rule a returned string gets), `text/plain` otherwise, an empty chunk included. With no such chunk (no body, a HEAD request, status 204 or 304, or a first chunk that is not UTF-8) none is added, and one the script set earlier stays. The rest of an answer whose headers the script already sent keeps them. A hook script's `metadata.hook.forward()` relays the upstream's status, headers and body, less the hop-by-hop ones; when the upstream cannot be reached, a synchronous `onUpstreamError` fallback that returns an object answers instead with the status it returns (502 unless it is an integer from 100 to 599), its headers less invalid and hop-by-hop ones, `text/plain` when it sets no Content-Type, an `X-Hoody-Hook-Audit` header, and its body when that is a string or Buffer (an empty body otherwise). A path ending in `.md` returns that documentation file instead of running a script; one beside a script is served under that script's `@enabled` and `@token`.

204.description: The script returned nothing and set no status. No body.

400.description: The service refused the request, the value the script returned, or the hoody-sdk in the scripts directory. A script can also answer with this status itself, with any body and Content-Type; the bodies below are the ones the service sends. The path is malformed: `Bad Request: URL path contains invalid percent-encoding.` or `Bad Request: URL path contains disallowed characters.` A proxy hook cannot send the client's own path to the upstream as written: it has a `.` or `..` segment (`%2e` forms included) or starts with `//`. `metadata.hook.forward()` answers so, and so does the service when `metadata.hook.fetchUpstream()` refused the path and the script then failed instead of answering. The body is `bad request path`, with `Cache-Control: no-store` and an `X-Hoody-Hook-Audit` header. The hostname is malformed: an HTML page headed `400 Bad Request` naming the problem. The body does not parse as its Content-Type: `{"error": "Invalid request body", "contentType": …}`. A script with `@rawBody` reads the body itself and never gets this. The script uses `@return-type-mode dev`, the service does not run in production, and the script returned a value that does not match its `@return-type`: `{"error": "Return type validation failed", "details": …, "expected": …, "actual": …}`. The same mismatch is a 500 in `strict` mode (the default) and in `dev` mode in production; `warn` mode only logs it and sends the value. The scripts directory holds a hoody-sdk from before the computer names, so the `hoody` global refused to build a client: no request was sent to any API. Upgrade the SDK in the scripts directory with the install command the message names (`npm i hoody-sdk@<version>`). The request's `Accept` names `application/json` and not `text/html`: the management API's error envelope, `{"error": <message>, "code": "upgrade_required", "details": {"code": "upgrade_required"}, "timestamp"}`. The same refusal to a request whose `Accept` does not ask for JSON: the sentence `VM Error in script '<name>': <message>` followed by ` (code upgrade_required)`.

404.description: No script answered this path. A script can also answer with this status itself, with any body and Content-Type; the bodies below are the ones the service sends. Nothing matches this hostname and path: an HTML page headed `404 Not Found` listing the script paths it tried, in priority order, and under "Did you mean" links to up to 3 routes of the same scope near the path (see `suggestions` in the JSON body). On an exclusive execId origin (an `.exclusive` marker in its deployment directory) only that directory is searched, with no fallbacks. A request whose `Accept` names `application/json` and not `text/html` gets the JSON body instead (`Vary: Accept`). Nothing matches this hostname and path, and the request's `Accept` names `application/json` and not `text/html`: the management API's error envelope, `{"error": "No script found for <path>", "code": "ERROR_404", "details": {"code": "SCRIPT_NOT_FOUND", …}, "timestamp"}`, with the same facts as the page, `tried` listing the script paths it tried in priority order and `suggestions` the routes near the path; when there is one, the `error` sentence ends `Did you mean <path>?` (several joined with ` or `). A matching script is disabled with `@enabled false`: `Not Found`. A `.md` path with no file, a system-prompt file (`<script>.system.md`, `_system.md`), or a file beside a disabled script: `Documentation not found: <path>`. A proxy hook dispatched the request and its target path has no script of its own (dynamic and catch-all routes and the index fallbacks never answer a hook): `hook target not found`, with `Cache-Control: no-store`.

anyOf.description: Nothing matches this hostname and path, and the request's `Accept` names `application/json` and not `text/html`: the management API's error envelope, `{"error": "No script found for <path>", "code": "ERROR_404", "details": {"code": "SCRIPT_NOT_FOUND", …}, "timestamp"}`, with the same facts as the page, `tried` listing the script paths it tried in priority order and `suggestions` the routes near the path; when there is one, the `error` sentence ends `Did you mean <path>?` (several joined with ` or `).

500.description: The script could not run to completion. A script can also answer with this status itself, with any body and Content-Type; the bodies below are the ones the service sends. It failed to load (compile, or install its dependencies): an HTML page titled `500 Script Compilation Error - Hoody Exec`, the parser's message (and its line in the file, when it can be traced back) first. A request whose `Accept` names `application/json` and not `text/html` gets the JSON body instead (`Vary: Accept`). It failed to load, and the request's `Accept` names `application/json` and not `text/html`: the management API's error envelope, `{"error": "Script failed to load: <message> (line <n>)", "code": "ERROR_500", "details": {"code": "SCRIPT_COMPILE_ERROR", "script", "message", "line"}, "timestamp"}`, `line` only when it can be traced back to the file. It threw, or broke its `@return-type` in `strict` mode or in `dev` mode in production: a plain sentence, `VM Error in script '<name>': <message>` or `Timeout: Script '<name>'`, followed by ` (code <code>, upstream status <status>)` when the thrown value carries a string `code` or an HTTP `status` / `statusCode` (an SDK ApiError, `ERR_VERSIONED_SPECIFIER`). A request whose `Accept` names `application/json` and not `text/html` gets the JSON body instead (`Vary: Accept`). It threw (as for the plain sentence `VM Error in script '<name>': <message>` or `Timeout: Script '<name>'`), and the request's `Accept` names `application/json` and not `text/html`: the management API's error envelope, `{"error": <that sentence>, "code": "ERROR_500", "details": {"code": …, "upstreamStatus": …}, "timestamp"}`. `details.code` is the thrown value's own string `code` (an SDK ApiError's, `ERR_VERSIONED_SPECIFIER`), else `SCRIPT_TIMEOUT` or `SCRIPT_ERROR`; `upstreamStatus` its HTTP `status` / `statusCode`, when it has one. The status stays 500, except for `upgrade_required`, which is the 400 answer. The service failed while handling the request: `Internal Server Error.`, sent without a Content-Type unless the script had already set one. It returned an `Error`: `{"error": <its message>}`. The deployment directory for this hostname and execId could not be checked for its `.exclusive` marker (a storage error other than not-found), so no script or `.md` file is served: `{"error": "Route scope unreadable", "code": "ROUTE_SCOPE_UNREADABLE", "message": …}`. A `.md` path whose companion script could not be read: `Internal Server Error`.

anyOf.description: It failed to load, and the request's `Accept` names `application/json` and not `text/html`: the management API's error envelope, `{"error": "Script failed to load: <message> (line <n>)", "code": "ERROR_500", "details": {"code": "SCRIPT_COMPILE_ERROR", "script", "message", "line"}, "timestamp"}`, `line` only when it can be traced back to the file.

502.description: A proxy hook's `metadata.hook.forward()` could not reach the upstream. A hook script's `onUpstreamError` fallback can answer with a status of its own instead; one whose status is not an integer from 100 to 599 is sent as 502 with its own headers and body, and one that returns a value other than an object (a string, a number) is sent as 502 with an empty body. A script can also answer with this status itself, with any body and Content-Type; the bodies below are the ones the service sends. The upstream request failed (network error, abort or timeout) before any answer was sent, and the hook script gave no usable `onUpstreamError` fallback (none, or one that threw, returned nothing or returned a Promise): `upstream unavailable`, with an `X-Hoody-Hook-Audit` header.

504.description: A time limit ran out before the script answered. The connection is closed, and a script that had started may still be running. A script can also answer with this status itself, with any body and Content-Type; the bodies below are the ones the service sends. The script's `@timeout` ran out: `{"error": "Script timeout", "timeoutMs": …}` with the limit. It is 60 minutes when the script sets none, and `@timeout 0` turns it off. It counts waiting for a free slot, loading the script (including installing its dependencies) and reading the request body, so the script may never have started. A proxy hook dispatched the request and its deadline ran out: `{"error": "hook timeout"}`, with no `timeoutMs`.

parameters.description: List all revisions of a file recorded in the journal. post.description: Check that TypeScript code transpiles, as the runtime transpiles it, and, with `typecheck: true`, type-check it against the installed hoody-sdk.

valid.description: The code transpiles (a syntax error is a 400) and, when it was type-checked, has no type error. Without `typecheck` it is always true.

typeChecked.description: True when the code was type-checked: `typecheck: true` was sent and the TypeScript compiler ran. Otherwise false: the code is only transpiled, types are stripped and never checked, so a type error is not reported.

diagnostics.description: Present when typeChecked is true. TypeScript errors, at most 50, on the lines of the code as sent. An import TypeScript cannot resolve (a package without types, a relative helper, a Node built-in) is not reported; its values are `any`.

line.description: 1-based line of the code as sent.

code.description: TypeScript error code (2339: a property that does not exist, 2551: the same with a suggestion, 2345: a wrong argument, …).

message.description: The compiler's message; follow-up lines are joined with `\n`. Its wording is not a stable contract.

source.description: The text of that line, trimmed; a line over 200 characters is cut to 200 around the column (`…` where cut).

hint.description: Present on the first 10 diagnostics that are on a hoody-sdk access or call (`hoody.files.list`, a client bound from `await hoody.withComputer(…)` or `new HoodyClient()`) with code 2339, 2551, 2345, 2554, 2559, 2741 or 2353, or 2322 inside an argument of an SDK call: what the installed SDK has there. `hoody` is the injected client only where no parameter, import or declaration shadows it. Best effort: an access the check cannot follow (a name assigned again, a value from another call) gets no hint.

access.description: The access recognised, from `hoody`: `hoody.files.list` (for the await note, the expression as written).

path.description: What the method is called on: `hoody.files`, `hoody.api.computers`, `hoody` for the client.

signature.description: The declaration, whitespace collapsed, at most 1500 characters. The URL-template and request-option parameters every kit method ends with are shown as `{ … }`.

summary.description: First paragraph of the method's doc comment (empty when it has none).

example.description: The doc comment's `@example`, else a call built from the required parameters, with the required fields of an object parameter (the first union alternative read whole); `(…)` for arguments the index cannot fill: an incomplete parameter, or a required object parameter with no required field.

file.description: The declaring `.d.ts`, relative to the package directory.

params.description: The parameters in order.

name.description: The declared name; a rest parameter whose type spells its positions (`...args: Parameters<F>`, a tuple) is listed as those positions, by their names.

type.description: The declared type, whitespace collapsed, at most 200 characters; `{ … }` for the URL-template and request-option parameters.

optional.description: True for an optional or defaulted parameter and a rest parameter of array type; a rest parameter whose positions cannot be read is not optional (it is `incomplete`).

fields.description: Present when the type is an object type written inline or declared in the SDK (an interface with its bases, a type alias of an object with its type arguments, an intersection or union, `Omit` / `Pick` / `Partial` / `Required` of those, `Parameters<…>[n]`): its fields one level deep, required ones first, at most 30.

type.description: The declared type, whitespace collapsed, at most 120 characters.

optional.description: True unless every alternative of the type requires the field (see `anyOf`).

requiredIn.description: Present when some alternatives of a union type require the field and others do not (`optional` is then true); `anyOf` names which.

doc.description: First paragraph of the field's doc comment, at most 200 characters (absent when it has none).

fieldsOmitted.description: Fields left out past the first 30 (absent when none).

anyOf.description: Present for a union of object types (also inside an intersection: `{ password } & ({ username } | { email })`): the required fields of each alternative. A call passes every field of one of them.

magicComments.description: Directives parsed from the script, keyed by directive name. Secret values are `[REDACTED]`. `token` is a single string, `[REDACTED]` when the script sets any `@token`, and `tokens` is always present: one `[REDACTED]` per `@token` line, `[]` when there is none. Durations (`timeout`, `schedule-timeout`) are numbers of milliseconds (`@timeout 30s` parses to 30000).

warnings.description: Directives whose value was present but unusable: a number with an unknown unit, trailing garbage or out of range, a value outside a directive's allowed set (`@mode banana`), a `@cors` value that is not reflective, `*`, none or one origin (prose such as `// @cors above …`), a `@cors-methods` / `@cors-headers` value that is not a comma-separated list of names, an `@ai-model` / `@ai-key` value with spaces or control characters, or a `@remote-token` that can never match (a line that does not parse, or a literal secret shorter than 16 characters). Such a line sets nothing: an earlier line of the directive still applies, else the default (an invalid `@remote-token` stays declared and matches nothing). Also listed: an origin read without its trailing `/`, and a directive set again on a later line to another value (the last one applies).

typeChecked.description: True when the code was type-checked: `typecheck: true` was sent and the TypeScript compiler ran. Otherwise false: the code is only transpiled, types are stripped and never checked, so a type error is not reported.

Such a line sets nothing: an earlier line of the directive still applies, else the default (an invalid `@remote-token` stays declared and matches nothing). Also listed: an origin read without its trailing `/`, and a directive set again on a later line to another value (the last one applies).

typecheck.description: Present with `typecheck: true` when the syntax is valid; `valid` false when it found a type error. The type check `typecheck: true` asked for: the TypeScript compiler run on the code as sent against the installed hoody-sdk declarations and the injected script globals (`hoody`, `req`, `res`, …).

diagnostics.description: TypeScript errors, at most 50, on the lines of the code as sent. An import TypeScript cannot resolve (a package without types, a relative helper, a Node built-in) is not reported; its values are `any`.

line.description: 1-based line of the code as sent.

code.description: TypeScript error code (2339: a property that does not exist, 2551: the same with a suggestion, 2345: a wrong argument, …).

message.description: The compiler's message; follow-up lines are joined with `\n`. Its wording is not a stable contract.

source.description: The text of that line, trimmed; a line over 200 characters is cut to 200 around the column (`…` where cut).

hint.description: Present on the first 10 diagnostics that are on a hoody-sdk access or call (`hoody.files.list`, a client bound from `await hoody.withComputer(…)` or `new HoodyClient()`) with code 2339, 2551, 2345, 2554, 2559, 2741 or 2353, or 2322 inside an argument of an SDK call: what the installed SDK has there. `hoody` is the injected client only where no parameter, import or declaration shadows it. Best effort: an access the check cannot follow (a name assigned again, a value from another call) gets no hint.

access.description: The access recognised, from `hoody`: `hoody.files.list` (for the await note, the expression as written).

path.description: What the method is called on: `hoody.files`, `hoody.api.computers`, `hoody` for the client.

signature.description: The declaration, whitespace collapsed, at most 1500 characters. The URL-template and request-option parameters every kit method ends with are shown as `{ … }`.

summary.description: First paragraph of the method's doc comment (empty when it has none).

example.description: The doc comment's `@example`, else a call built from the required parameters, with the required fields of an object parameter (the first union alternative read whole); `(…)` for arguments the index cannot fill: an incomplete parameter, or a required object parameter with no required field.

file.description: The declaring `.d.ts`, relative to the package directory.

params.description: The parameters in order.

name.description: The declared name; a rest parameter whose type spells its positions (`...args: Parameters<F>`, a tuple) is listed as those positions, by their names.

type.description: The declared type, whitespace collapsed, at most 200 characters; `{ … }` for the URL-template and request-option parameters.

optional.description: True for an optional or defaulted parameter and a rest parameter of array type; a rest parameter whose positions cannot be read is not optional (it is `incomplete`).

fields.description: Present when the type is an object type written inline or declared in the SDK (an interface with its bases, a type alias of an object with its type arguments, an intersection or union, `Omit` / `Pick` / `Partial` / `Required` of those, `Parameters<…>[n]`): its fields one level deep, required ones first, at most 30.

type.description: The declared type, whitespace collapsed, at most 120 characters.

optional.description: True unless every alternative of the type requires the field (see `anyOf`).

requiredIn.description: Present when some alternatives of a union type require the field and others do not (`optional` is then true); `anyOf` names which.

doc.description: First paragraph of the field's doc comment, at most 200 characters (absent when it has none).

fieldsOmitted.description: Fields left out past the first 30 (absent when none).

anyOf.description: Present for a union of object types (also inside an intersection: `{ password } & ({ username } | { email })`): the required fields of each alternative. A call passes every field of one of them.

candidates.description: For a name the object does not have: up to 3 nearest methods (or namespaces) on it, by name and summary words.

namespace.description: Set instead of `method` for a namespace (`hoody.sqlite`).

note.description: A fix in words: the object is the Promise of `hoody.withComputer(…)`, which needs `await`.

truncated.description: Errors left out of `diagnostics` past the first 50.

sdkVersion.description: Version of the hoody-sdk copy in `<scripts>/node_modules` the check used; null when there is none (then `hoody` is untyped).

language.description: validate/script only: the language the code was checked as.

message.description: validate/script only: `No type errors` when `valid`, else `<n> type error(s); first at line <line>: <message>`.

error.description: Present when `typecheck: true` was sent but the check could not run (no TypeScript 7 compiler and its install failed, a timeout, …); `typeChecked` is then false and `valid` reflects the transpile only. Its wording is not a stable contract.

publishable.description: True when scripts/write (with validation on) would accept this code: `blocking` is empty.

blocking.description: What scripts/write would refuse this code for; empty when it is publishable. A type error blocks only when `typecheck: true` was sent and the check ran.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: Script path relative to the scripts directory, for example `api/users.js`. Under the call's scope (`execId` / `exec_id` / `subdomain`, else the Host's `[<subdomain>.]…-exec-<execId>`) it is read as `<subdomain|default>/<execId>/<path>` unless it already starts with that prefix. Leading slashes are dropped (a path inside the scripts directory is made relative to it), so an absolute computer path such as `/home/user/file.txt` names a file under the scripts directory, not on the computer.

parameters.name: execId
parameters.description: Optional execution scope. When provided, relative paths resolve under default/{execId}/ unless subdomain is also set. Query value takes precedence over body. Lowercase alphanumeric, no hyphens: the `-exec-` part of a hostname cannot carry one, so a hyphenated execId names a tree no request could route to and is rejected with 400.

path.description: Path

resolvedPath.description: Resolved Path

magicComments.description: Directives parsed from the script, keyed by directive name. Secret values are `[REDACTED]`. `token` is a single string, `[REDACTED]` when the script sets any `@token`, and `tokens` is always present: one `[REDACTED]` per `@token` line, `[]` when there is none. Durations (`timeout`, `schedule-timeout`) are numbers of milliseconds (`@timeout 30s` parses to 30000).

remote.description: How to reach this script's remote operations (send, call, eval, events, attach) on its own URL. Every operation is off by default and switched on by a magic comment; this summary never carries a secret.

enabled.description: True when at least one remote operation is switched on.

ops.description: Which operations the magic comments switch on: `@remote-messages` (send, events, attach), `@remote-call` and `@remote-eval`.

gate.description: What guards send, call and events: the script's `@remote-token`s (`remote-token`), else its `@token` (`script-token`), else nothing (`open`). Eval always needs an eval-scoped `@remote-token`.

token_names.description: Names of the script's `@remote-token`s. Never their secrets.

token_ready.description: True when a `@remote-token` with the `eval` scope is declared. Whether an `env:` secret resolves is known only when the operation runs.

route.description: The script's route inside its deployment (`[param]` segments as written), or null when the file is outside the call's deployment tree or `routable` is false.

url.description: The script's public URL, segments percent-encoded (a `[param]` placeholder keeps its brackets), or null when the management call's Host does not name the box, the file is outside the call's deployment tree, or `routable` is false.

routable.description: False when the script's path holds a character the router refuses in a URL path (only A-Z a-z 0-9 - _ . / pass; a `[param]` segment is exempt): no URL can reach it, and scripts/write and scripts/move no longer create such a name.

connect.description: Present when an operation is on: the request header naming the operation, the operations it takes, and for `@remote-messages` the EventSource query and the WebSocket subprotocol.

revision.description: An opaque revision of the stored bytes (16 lowercase hex): it changes whenever the bytes change, and is compared only with revisions from the same kit.

value.description: The value as written (a secret shown as [REDACTED])

message.description: Why it is unusable and what applies instead

magicCommentWarnings.description: Present only for a .ts/.js script with warnings. Directives whose value was present but unusable: a number with an unknown unit, trailing garbage or out of range, a value outside a directive's allowed set (`@mode banana`), a `@cors` value that is not reflective, `*`, none or one origin (prose such as `// @cors above …`), a `@cors-methods` / `@cors-headers` value that is not a comma-separated list of names, an `@ai-model` / `@ai-key` value with spaces or control characters, or a `@remote-token` that can never match (a line that does not parse, or a literal secret shorter than 16 characters). Such a line sets nothing: an earlier line of the directive still applies, else the default (an invalid `@remote-token` stays declared and matches nothing). Also listed: an origin read without its trailing `/`, and a directive set again on a later line to another value (the last one applies). The file is written either way.

normalizationWarnings.description: Present only for a validated .ts/.js script with warnings. Code that runs other than it reads, naming its lines: a `return` alone on its line with the value on the next line. A plain value there is returned (it is listed in `transformations` too); any other statement is reported and left as written (it never runs). The file is written either way.

typeChecked.description: Present only with `typecheck: true` on a validated .js/.ts write: true when the type check ran (and found no error, or the write would have been refused with 400), false when it could not run (`typecheck.error` says why; the file is written).

typecheck.description: Present only with `typecheck: true` on a validated .js/.ts write. The type check `typecheck: true` asked for: the TypeScript compiler run on the code as sent against the installed hoody-sdk declarations and the injected script globals (`hoody`, `req`, `res`, …).

diagnostics.description: TypeScript errors, at most 50, on the lines of the code as sent. An import TypeScript cannot resolve (a package without types, a relative helper, a Node built-in) is not reported; its values are `any`.

line.description: 1-based line of the code as sent.

code.description: TypeScript error code (2339: a property that does not exist, 2551: the same with a suggestion, 2345: a wrong argument, …).

message.description: The compiler's message; follow-up lines are joined with `\n`. Its wording is not a stable contract.

source.description: The text of that line, trimmed; a line over 200 characters is cut to 200 around the column (`…` where cut).

hint.description: Present on the first 10 diagnostics that are on a hoody-sdk access or call (`hoody.files.list`, a client bound from `await hoody.withComputer(…)` or `new HoodyClient()`) with code 2339, 2551, 2345, 2554, 2559, 2741 or 2353, or 2322 inside an argument of an SDK call: what the installed SDK has there. `hoody` is the injected client only where no parameter, import or declaration shadows it. Best effort: an access the check cannot follow (a name assigned again, a value from another call) gets no hint.

access.description: The access recognised, from `hoody`: `hoody.files.list` (for the await note, the expression as written).

path.description: What the method is called on: `hoody.files`, `hoody.api.computers`, `hoody` for the client.

signature.description: The declaration, whitespace collapsed, at most 1500 characters. The URL-template and request-option parameters every kit method ends with are shown as `{ … }`.

summary.description: First paragraph of the method's doc comment (empty when it has none).

example.description: The doc comment's `@example`, else a call built from the required parameters, with the required fields of an object parameter (the first union alternative read whole); `(…)` for arguments the index cannot fill: an incomplete parameter, or a required object parameter with no required field.

file.description: The declaring `.d.ts`, relative to the package directory.

params.description: The parameters in order.

name.description: The declared name; a rest parameter whose type spells its positions (`...args: Parameters<F>`, a tuple) is listed as those positions, by their names.

type.description: The declared type, whitespace collapsed, at most 200 characters; `{ … }` for the URL-template and request-option parameters.

optional.description: True for an optional or defaulted parameter and a rest parameter of array type; a rest parameter whose positions cannot be read is not optional (it is `incomplete`).

fields.description: Present when the type is an object type written inline or declared in the SDK (an interface with its bases, a type alias of an object with its type arguments, an intersection or union, `Omit` / `Pick` / `Partial` / `Required` of those, `Parameters<…>[n]`): its fields one level deep, required ones first, at most 30.

type.description: The declared type, whitespace collapsed, at most 120 characters.

optional.description: True unless every alternative of the type requires the field (see `anyOf`).

requiredIn.description: Present when some alternatives of a union type require the field and others do not (`optional` is then true); `anyOf` names which.

doc.description: First paragraph of the field's doc comment, at most 200 characters (absent when it has none).

fieldsOmitted.description: Fields left out past the first 30 (absent when none).

anyOf.description: Present for a union of object types (also inside an intersection: `{ password } & ({ username } | { email })`): the required fields of each alternative. A call passes every field of one of them.

incomplete.description: Present when part of the type could not be read (an intersection part or base the index cannot follow, a rest parameter whose positions it cannot tell, a type past the work budget of the index): `fields` may miss some, required ones included. `example` is then built from the first alternative read whole, else `(…)`.

method.description: The method called, as GET sdk-types lists it (its first overload): signature, summary, example and parameter fields.

overloads.description: Signatures of the method's other overloads.

candidates.description: For a name the object does not have: up to 3 nearest methods (or namespaces) on it, by name and summary words.

signature.description: At most 300 characters; GET sdk-types has it whole.

namespace.description: Set instead of `method` for a namespace (`hoody.sqlite`).

note.description: A fix in words: the object is the Promise of `hoody.withComputer(…)`, which needs `await`.

truncated.description: Errors left out of `diagnostics` past the first 50.

sdkVersion.description: Version of the hoody-sdk copy in `<scripts>/node_modules` the check used; null when there is none (then `hoody` is untyped).

language.description: validate/script only: the language the code was checked as.

message.description: validate/script only: `No type errors` when `valid`, else `<n> type error(s); first at line <line>: <message>`.

error.description: Present when `typecheck: true` was sent but the check could not run (no TypeScript 7 compiler and its install failed, a timeout, …); `typeChecked` is then false and `valid` reflects the transpile only. Its wording is not a stable contract.

revision.description: The stored bytes' revision after the write (`[REDACTED]` placeholders resolved). Send it as `ifRevision` with the next change.

previousRevision.description: The revision this write replaced; null when it created the file.

op.description: Present only when the request sent `opId`: the journal's receipt for this change.

outcome.description: Always `committed` on a success answer.

replayed.description: True when this answer is the stored outcome of an earlier request with the same `opId` (the change was not made again).

schema.description: A resend of an `opId` the journal already holds as committed answers the stored file facts and revisions again without making the change again (`op.replayed` true); the reports made while writing (`remote`, `env`, `schedule`, the warnings, `typecheck`) are not repeated.

resolvedPath.description: The path after the execId/subdomain scope is applied, relative to the scripts directory.

path.description: Script path relative to the scripts directory, for example `api/users.js`. Under the call's scope (`execId` / `exec_id` / `subdomain`, else the Host's `[<subdomain>.]…-exec-<execId>`) it is read as `<subdomain|default>/<execId>/<path>` unless it already starts with that prefix. Leading slashes are dropped (a path inside the scripts directory is made relative to it), so an absolute computer path such as `/home/user/file.txt` names a file under the scripts directory, not on the computer.

content.description: Content. `scripts/read` shows `@token` / `@ai-key` values (and an SDK marker's `magic_comments.token`) as `[REDACTED]`; written back, each placeholder keeps the stored value it stands for (the n-th such directive line takes the stored file's n-th). In a `.js` / `.ts` script or a `.sdk.json` marker, a placeholder with no stored value (a new file, or no matching line) is refused with 400 and `details.code` `REDACTED_SECRET_UNRESOLVED`; the placeholder is never stored as a secret.

ifNotExists.description: Create only. When true and the name already exists as anything (a file, a directory, a live or dangling symlink, which is never followed), nothing is written and the answer is 409; a symlinked ancestor directory is still 403. The existence check and the create are one atomic step, so of several concurrent creates (from any process) exactly one succeeds. A failed create is 500 with `details.code` `CREATE_FAILED` (nothing published); a create that published the file but could not remove its temporary name is 500 with `details.code` `CREATED_CLEANUP_FAILED` and that name in `details.leftover`.

typecheck.description: When true, also type-check the code with the TypeScript compiler against the hoody-sdk declarations in `<scripts>/node_modules` and the script globals (`hoody`, `req`, `res`, …). Imports TypeScript cannot resolve are not reported; types from relative helper files are not checked (`any`). The first check on a scripts directory without TypeScript 7 installs it there. Only with validation on, for a .js/.ts path: a type error refuses the write with 400 (`details.validation.typecheck.diagnostics`); a check that could not run does not.

execId.description: Optional execution scope in request body. Query execId/exec_id takes precedence when both are provided. Lowercase alphanumeric, no hyphens: the `-exec-` part of a hostname cannot carry one, so a hyphenated execId names a tree no request could route to and is rejected with 400.

exec_id.description: Alias for execId (snake_case). Lowercase alphanumeric, no hyphens: the `-exec-` part of a hostname cannot carry one, so a hyphenated execId names a tree no request could route to and is rejected with 400.

subdomain.description: Optional subdomain namespace used with execId for path resolution.

ifRevision.description: Write only over this revision (from scripts/read); null means create only (like `ifNotExists`). A different current revision is 409 `REVISION_MISMATCH`, nothing written. Not with `ifNotExists`.

opId.description: Journals the change under this id (16-64 letters, digits, `_` or `-`). Resending the identical request with the same id after it finished answers the stored outcome without changing anything again. Reusing the id for a different request is 409 `OP_ID_REUSED`; an operation not yet finished answers 409 `OP_IN_PROGRESS` or `OP_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN`, and one ops/settle settled as never received answers 409 `OP_FENCED`. ops/settle tells what became of it when the answer was lost.

expectRoute.description: Refuse the change (409 `ROUTE_EFFECT_CHANGED`, nothing done) unless, after it, this URL path is still answered by `answeredBy`. route/resolve with `omit` previews a delete.

answeredBy.description: The script expected to answer, relative to the scripts root; null when no script should.

note.description: A short note kept with the version this change writes (one line, at most 120 printable characters).

servers.description: The computer's exec kit: projectId and computerId name the computer, server the server that hosts it, and serviceIndex the kit instance (1-9999).

delete.description: Delete a script file; a symlink at the name (live or dangling) is removed itself, never followed.

post.description: Resolve a URL path to the script file that handles it, exactly as script execution would. Supports static routes, dynamic segments [param], catch-all [...slug], and optional catch-all [[...path]]. Routes are matched in priority order: static > dynamic > catch-all > optional catch-all. Scoped by hostname and execId: checks {hostname}/{execId}/, then {hostname}/, then {execId}/, then root. When no route matches, the runtime's fallback scripts apply in order: {hostname}.ts/.js, {hostname}/index.ts/.js, then the root index.ts/.js. When {hostname}/{execId}/ holds an `.exclusive` marker file, only that directory is searched and no fallback applies. hostname and execId are lowercased, as the runtime does. A marker that cannot be read is a 500 with details.code ROUTE_SCOPE_UNREADABLE. Returns the matched script path, extracted route parameters, and route type (static, dynamic, catchall, optional-catchall, or fallback). When nothing matches, `suggestions` lists up to 3 routes of the same scope near the path (leading folders dropped, or a folder of the deployment added), each with the script it runs.

post.description: Discover all available routes in the script directory, classified by Next.js-style type. Scans for .js and .ts files and classifies each as: static, dynamic ([param]), catch-all ([...slug]), or optional catch-all ([[...path]]). Returns the route pattern (relative to baseDir), file path, type, and extracted parameter names for each route, and `route`: the URL path on which the runtime serves that file for the request's scope (hostname and execId, from the body or else the Host header, as in route/resolve), or null when no route could be verified: no URL reaches it in that scope, or (rarely, a URL may then still reach it) routes overlap past the checking budget. Optionally includes file metadata (size, modification time) when includeMetadata is true.

baseDir.description: `baseDir` is returned as given, or as `/` when omitted or empty.

hostname.description: The hostname scope `route` was computed for (body `hostname`, else the Host header's subdomain, else `default`; lowercased).

execId.description: The execId scope `route` was computed for (body `execId`, else the Host header's; lowercased), or null for none.

pattern.description: The route pattern relative to baseDir (the scripts root when none is given), with a leading slash and `[param]` segments as written, for example `/api/users/[id]`. Not a URL unless baseDir is the deployment's own directory: `route` is.

route.description: The URL path on which the runtime serves this file for the request's scope (hostname and execId, from the body or else the Host header), `[param]` segments as written: fill each with your value, a catch-all with one or more segments ([[...x]]: none or more). Checked against the runtime's own order of routes, so the path reaches this file with any parameter value that is not the name of another route at that position (and, in the last segment, does not end in .js or .ts, which the router drops); a value or a catch-all segment count that a narrower route also matches goes to that route, which is listed with its own `route`. The path inside the most specific search directory of the scope is preferred (`/x`, then `/x/index` for an index file, then the name with its extension: `/x.ts.ts`, `/..ts`); a file the deployment's own tree shadows can still answer through a wider one (`/default/x`). null when no route could be verified, which is mostly when no URL reaches the file in this scope: other routes take every URL it matches (alone or together), it is outside an exclusive tree, its path holds a character the router refuses, it is a `.js` beside its `.ts` twin, a search directory of the scope is a symlink, or (the one case where a URL may still reach it) the routes overlap so much that checking this one would take more than a fixed amount of work. A file that only the hostname or root index fallback serves is null too. When unsure the answer is null, never a path that serves another file.

execId.description: Exec ID the SDK is imported under: 1 to 64 lowercase letters or digits. When omitted, it is taken from the Host header.

source_url.description: HTTPS URL of the OpenAPI document to import. It must name a domain (not an IP address), use port 443, and end in `.json`, `.yaml`, `/documentation/json` or `/documentation/yaml`.

source_auth.description: Credentials sent when fetching `source_url`: either `{"type": "bearer", "token": "…"}` or `{"type": "basic", "username": "…", "password": "…"}`. Credentials that could not be sent as given are refused with a 400, never dropped. Other members are ignored.

type.description: `bearer` sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; `basic` sends HTTP Basic credentials built from `username` and `password`.

token.description: Bearer token: printable characters (ASCII or Latin-1) with no surrounding whitespace. Required when `type` is `bearer`.

username.description: Basic-auth user name, without a colon. Required when `type` is `basic`.

password.description: Basic-auth password. Required when `type` is `basic`.

middleware.description: Middleware written next to the generated proxy files. Each member is JavaScript source, written as `pre.js` or `post.js` into every directory that receives a proxy. A member that is omitted, `null` or an empty string sends no new source: a re-import keeps the installed middleware, and a proxy directory that has none of that name gets a copy of the one at the SDK root. The source runs as the body of a function with `req` and `res` in scope; it is not a module, so do not `export` a function. Example: `req.headers["x-trace"] = "1";`.

pre.description: Source of `pre.js`, which runs before the generated proxies in its directory handle a request.

post.description: Source of `post.js`, which runs after the generated proxies in its directory handle a request.

magic_comments.description: Magic-comment directives written into every generated proxy file, keyed by directive name. Only the members listed here are accepted; any other key is refused with a 400, and so is a value that would not read back from the generated file as sent. When omitted or `null`, a re-import keeps the directives the previous import stored.

enabled.description: When false, the generated endpoints are written disabled. `null` is the same as omitting it.

token.description: Shared secret every generated endpoint requires; several (an array) are all accepted. A string for one token, or a non-empty array (at most 16, each different) for several; each a non-empty single word, with no whitespace and no control characters, and not `[REDACTED]`. `null` is the same as omitting it.

mode.description: Execution model. Default `serverless`. `null` is the same as omitting it.

timeout.description: Script timeout. `0` disables it. Default `30000`. Send an integer number of milliseconds (at most 2147483647), or a string: a duration such as `90s` or `5m` with at most 15 digits before and after any decimal point, leading zeros aside (a duration above 2147483647 ms, about 24.8 days, is read as that maximum), or one of `false`, `0`, `-1`, `unlimited`, `none`, `n/a`. `null` is the same as omitting it.

log-level.description: Request logging level. Default `standard`. `null` is the same as omitting it.

concurrent.description: Concurrency policy: `true`, `false`, or the maximum number of concurrent requests. `null` is the same as omitting it.

cors.description: CORS origin strategy, for example `reflective`. `none` disables CORS, and an empty string is the same as omitting it. A single word, with no whitespace. `null` is the same as omitting it.

websocket.description: When true, the generated files are written with WebSocket mode enabled. `null` is the same as omitting it.

force.description: Overwrite conflicting files (untracked files, and files changed since the last import) instead of answering 409 with a dry-run report.

parameters.name: kit
parameters.description: Kit to list: a client property (`files`, `api`, `exec`, `sqlite`, …), or `client` for the client's own methods (`withComputer`, `login`, …). Any letter case. An unknown kit is a 404 with `details.kits`.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description: Words, all of which must appear in the method's path, name or summary (any letter case).

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Most methods to return, 1 to 100 (default 20). `total` counts every match.

parameters.name: raw
parameters.description: When true, also return the `.d.ts` text of the files declaring the returned methods (`dts`, at most 256 KB). Needs `kit` or `q`.

sdkVersion.description: Version of the hoody-sdk copy in `<scripts>/node_modules`, the one scripts load.

kits.description: Every kit of the client with its method count. A kit is the client property the methods hang under (`files`, `api`, `exec`, …); `client` holds the client's own methods (`withComputer`, `login`, …).

total.description: Methods matching `kit` and `q` (0 when neither is given).

truncated.description: More methods matched than `limit` returned.

methods.description: Matching methods, best match first: a whole-name match, then a name containing a word, then the path, then the summary. An overloaded method has one entry per signature; methods the SDK adds by module augmentation (`files.readText`, …) are included.

path.description: What the method is called on: `hoody.files`, `hoody.api.computers`, `hoody` for the client.

signature.description: The declaration, whitespace collapsed, at most 1500 characters. The URL-template and request-option parameters every kit method ends with are shown as `{ … }`.

summary.description: First paragraph of the method's doc comment (empty when it has none).

example.description: The doc comment's `@example`, else a call built from the required parameters, with the required fields of an object parameter (the first union alternative read whole); `(…)` for arguments the index cannot fill: an incomplete parameter, or a required object parameter with no required field.

file.description: The declaring `.d.ts`, relative to the package directory.

params.description: The parameters in order.

name.description: The declared name; a rest parameter whose type spells its positions (`...args: Parameters<F>`, a tuple) is listed as those positions, by their names.

type.description: The declared type, whitespace collapsed, at most 200 characters; `{ … }` for the URL-template and request-option parameters.

optional.description: True for an optional or defaulted parameter and a rest parameter of array type; a rest parameter whose positions cannot be read is not optional (it is `incomplete`).

fields.description: Present when the type is an object type written inline or declared in the SDK (an interface with its bases, a type alias of an object with its type arguments, an intersection or union, `Omit` / `Pick` / `Partial` / `Required` of those, `Parameters<…>[n]`): its fields one level deep, required ones first, at most 30.

type.description: The declared type, whitespace collapsed, at most 120 characters.

optional.description: True unless every alternative of the type requires the field (see `anyOf`).

requiredIn.description: Present when some alternatives of a union type require the field and others do not (`optional` is then true); `anyOf` names which.

doc.description: First paragraph of the field's doc comment, at most 200 characters (absent when it has none).

fieldsOmitted.description: Fields left out past the first 30 (absent when none).

anyOf.description: Present for a union of object types (also inside an intersection: `{ password } & ({ username } | { email })`): the required fields of each alternative. A call passes every field of one of them.

incomplete.description: Present when part of the type could not be read (an intersection part or base the index cannot follow, a rest parameter whose positions it cannot tell, a type past the work budget of the index): `fields` may miss some, required ones included. `example` is then built from the first alternative read whole, else `(…)`.

dts.description: With `raw=true`: the `.d.ts` files declaring the returned methods, each headed by `// <file>`, at most 256 KB.

dtsOmitted.description: With `raw=true`: declaring files left out of `dts` to stay under 256 KB.

message.description: `<returned> of <total> matching method(s)`; `No method matches` when nothing matches; `Pass kit and/or q to list methods` when neither `kit` nor `q` is given.

warnings.description: Directives whose value was present but unusable: a number with an unknown unit, trailing garbage or out of range, a value outside a directive's allowed set (`@mode banana`), a `@cors` value that is not reflective, `*`, none or one origin (prose such as `// @cors above …`), a `@cors-methods` / `@cors-headers` value that is not a comma-separated list of names, an `@ai-model` / `@ai-key` value with spaces or control characters, or a `@remote-token` that can never match (a line that does not parse, or a literal secret shorter than 16 characters). Such a line sets nothing: an earlier line of the directive still applies, else the default (an invalid `@remote-token` stays declared and matches nothing). secret.description: Present on a secret directive, whose value is never returned.

redacted.description: Present when the line names a secret directive anywhere: no text read from it is returned (no `value`, no `raw`).

in_force.description: False when a later line overrides this one, or `@cors none` makes it inert. `@log-level` and `@debug true` set one log level, as the runtime reads them: the last of their lines is in force, either way round.

A key that is not a directive is 400 `UNKNOWN_DIRECTIVE`; `token`, `tokens`, `ai-key` and `remote-token` are 400 `SECRET_DIRECTIVE` (edit their lines in the code); a value the schema refuses is 400 `INVALID_VALUE`, and so is a CORS sub-directive set next to `cors: "none"`.

timeout.description: Script timeout. A bare number is MILLISECONDS (e.g. 30000); a unit suffix is honoured: ms, s, m, h, d (e.g. 90s, 5m). 0 disables timeout. Soft timeout on both HTTP and cron: in-flight VM work is not killed. Send an integer number of milliseconds (at most 2147483647), or a string: a duration such as `90s` or `5m` with at most 15 digits before and after any decimal point, leading zeros aside (a duration above 2147483647 ms, about 24.8 days, is read as that maximum), or one of `false`, `0`, `-1`, `unlimited`, `none`, `n/a`.
