put.description: Upload a file to the server or to a remote backend. Use ?append to append to existing file instead of overwriting. Use ?chmod to give a local file exact permission bits as part of the write. A new file is created no broader than the mode asked for. A replaced file is first narrowed to what both its current mode and the requested one allow; that is the restriction point. From then on its old content is readable under no broader bits than both modes allow, and the new content is published under the requested mode. A descriptor opened before the restriction point, including one opened while the body is being uploaded, keeps the access it was opened with. Uploads, appends and permission changes made through this server, by any name of the file, are serialized with the write; other processes writing the file directly are not. Servers that accept ?chmod list `put_chmod` in the `features` of GET /api/v1/version.

parameters.description: Backend ID for remote upload
parameters.name: backend

parameters.description: Append body to end of existing file (create if missing) instead of overwriting
parameters.name: append

parameters.description: Permission bits the local file ends with, in octal (`644`, `0600`, `0o755`, `000`), whatever the server's umask; the response gives them in `mode`, read back from the file. Where the filesystem keeps no permission bits of its own (a mount of a remote storage without them), the upload is answered 409 PERMISSIONS_NOT_APPLIED instead: nothing is changed when the bits asked for are narrower than the file's, and otherwise the body is written whole under the file's bits. Requires both upload and chmod to be enabled (403 otherwise). setuid, setgid and sticky bits are refused, as are values above 777. Refused with 400 together with `backend` or `append`, and when the path names something other than a regular file (a directory, a pipe, a device, a socket). Each of these refusals comes before the body is read: nothing is created or changed.
parameters.name: chmod

parameters.description: Create-time owner (user[:group]/uid[:gid]) for a newly-created file. Requires the deployment to have enabled chown and to permit the owner you name; refuses root. Overwrites/appends to an existing file preserve its owner. Absent → server default.
parameters.name: owner

parameters.description: The length of the whole body in bytes, for a body streamed without Content-Length. A body that ends before this many bytes, or runs past them, is refused with 400 and nothing is written or appended: the file stays as it was. Send it whenever the length is known: some HTTP/2 clients end a request's body normally when they are aborted, so without it a cut-off body can look complete. Over the upload size limit it is refused with 413 before the body is read.
parameters.name: X-Expected-Length

parameters.description: Local files only; with backend it is refused with 400. Write only if the file has this ETag (the one a download of it answers with; a weak ETag never matches), or with '*' only if a file exists at the path. Otherwise 412 and nothing is written or created.
parameters.name: If-Match

parameters.description: Local files only; with backend it is refused with 400. '*' writes only if nothing exists at the path (create only); a tag writes only if the file does not have that ETag. Otherwise 412 and nothing is written.
parameters.name: If-None-Match

parameters.description: Local files only; with backend it is refused with 400. Without If-Match, write only if the file has not changed since this HTTP date. Otherwise 412 and nothing is written.
parameters.name: If-Unmodified-Since

mode.description: The permission bits the file now has, in canonical octal (`755`, `600`, `0`). Present only when ?chmod was given.

400.description: The request cannot be carried out as asked: the body has fewer or more bytes than X-Expected-Length declared, or that header is not a whole number, the body of an upload addressed to a backend stopped arriving before it was complete (a dropped connection), the path names a directory, the path or one of its components cannot be used (too long, a symlink loop where symlinks are refused), or the owner given in ?owner is not usable. Nothing is written for an upload addressed to a backend. With ?chmod: the value is not octal permission bits, it carries setuid, setgid or sticky bits, it is combined with `backend` or `append`, or the path names something other than a regular file, each answered before the body is read, with nothing created or changed.

get.description: Query file mutation journal entries with optional filters. Supports cursor-based pagination via after_id. A page can hold fewer entries than limit, or none, while has_more is true: keep paging with next_after_id until has_more is false. The journal records only changes made through Hoody Files; a change made by the agent's tools, a terminal, a script or a program is not recorded.

post.description:
Create a FUSE filesystem mount for a connected backend, allowing direct file system access to remote storage. The mount is saved to be restored after a restart; a 201 does not guarantee restoration if saving failed. After a restart, a mount with settings of its own (vfs_config) comes back with status `error` and the message that it was not started after the restart; update it (PATCH /api/v1/mounts/{id}) to start it again. There is no separate 'persist' flag. To remove a mount, use DELETE /api/v1/mounts/{id}.

vfs_config sets custom VFS settings from the start, with the same fields and rules as PATCH /api/v1/mounts/{id}; fields you omit take their defaults. Custom settings are available only on the backend types PATCH /api/v1/mounts/{id} lists. A mount_path inside the server's own internal directories is refused with 400.

A file written through the mount is uploaded to the backend after the upload delay (vfs_config write_back). When the same file on the backend is also changed elsewhere in that time, the upload that reaches the backend last wins, even when it carries the older change, and neither side gets an error. Keep one writer per file on a mounted backend.

patch.description:
Change the settings of an existing mount: its VFS settings (vfs_config), and its auto_deliver setting. The update is partial: fields you omit keep their current value. The response carries the mount as it is afterwards. A mount listed as error because its saved settings were refused can be repaired with an update.

Every change of vfs_config restarts the mount; a change of auto_deliver alone does not. The mount path switches to the new settings at once, and new opens use them. Files already open keep the previous settings until they are closed. When the previous settings were custom, that holds until they are shut down: at the latest 24 hours after the switch, or sooner if their files cannot be checked for a minute, or their oldest unsent file is 24 hours old and their uploads are failing. When the previous settings were the defaults and no other mount uses the backend's shared connection, files still open stop working once that idle connection is closed. A program whose working directory is inside the mount must change into it again after the switch.

Files written and closed before the update must finish uploading before the switch, whatever the mount's current settings. They upload after the current upload delay (write_back; 5 seconds on the default settings). A mount on the default settings shares its upload queue with the backend's other default-settings mounts, so their closed files are waited for too. Files still open are not waited for. If the uploads have not finished within 10 seconds, the update is refused with 409 and nothing changes. The message says which case applies: the files are waiting for the upload delay, so retry after it; or they cannot be uploaded, so fix the backend or delete the mount. With switch=immediate the update does not wait for them: the new settings serve at once, and those files upload later with the previous settings, so such an upload can replace a newer write made through the new settings; previous_uploads_pending in the answer says how many files were still waiting. If those files cannot all be checked within the 10 seconds, the update is refused with 409 MOUNT_BUSY and nothing changes, rather than reporting a count it does not know.

A file that is open for writing across the switch is uploaded with the previous settings when it is closed. If the same file is also written through the new settings meanwhile, the upload that finishes last wins.

A service restart keeps the mount's uploads running: files written and closed before it finish uploading before the mount becomes available again, on default and custom settings alike, and files open across it upload when they close. If that takes over a minute, the mount stays unavailable with an error that says so; repeating the update, or reconnecting the backend, tries again. While those files are still uploading, an update or a new mount on the same backend waits for them, then answers 409. Before the machine or computer shuts down, the service waits a few seconds for closed files to upload.

Only a crash, a reboot or shutdown of the machine or computer, or the previous settings stopping on their own or being shut down by those limits, can leave files unsent. Those files are kept on the server and are not uploaded; the mount's pending_uploads counts them. They are never deleted without a request. While they fill their limit, custom settings are refused with 507.

An update of a mount that is still starting waits for it. Updates of mounts on the same backend are carried out one at a time. An update that cannot finish in time, behind the mount's start or another update, answers 409 MOUNT_BUSY with Retry-After, and nothing changes.

read_only applies to the mount path only; the backend file API can still write.

A file written through the mount is uploaded to the backend after the upload delay (write_back). When the same file on the backend is also changed elsewhere in that time, the upload that reaches the backend last wins, even when it carries the older change, and neither side gets an error. Keep one writer per file on a mounted backend.

Sending the settings the mount already has changes nothing: the answer is 200 with remounted: false. A mount set back to all the defaults shares its backend's cache again, so changes made through other mounts or through the backend file API appear at once.

If the mount cannot start with the new settings, for example because the backend refuses its credentials, the answer is 502 and the mount keeps its previous settings.

Custom settings are available for these backend types: azureblob, azurefiles, b2, drive, dropbox, fichier, filescom, ftp, gofile, google cloud storage, google photos, hdfs, http, imagekit, internetarchive, koofr, mega, netstorage, opendrive, oracleobjectstorage, pcloud, pixeldrain, qingstor, quatrix, s3, seafile, sftp, sia, smb, swift, webdav. Other backend types answer 400 and keep the default settings.

delete.description:
Remove a mount and disconnect the FUSE filesystem. A mount that is still mounting is removed at once. `uploads` says what becomes of what was written on the mount and is not uploaded yet:

- `keep` (the default): a mount with a `vfs_config` of its own keeps uploading it in the background after the answer, and files still open on the mount keep working until they are closed. That goes on until nothing is held open and nothing is left to upload, for at most 24 hours; what is left then is kept on the server and is not uploaded. A mount served by its backend's shared connection, which no other mount uses and which holds files not uploaded yet or open: the answer waits while they upload, at most about 35 seconds (longer with a larger `write_back`), and what is left then is kept on the server as a pending upload, listed before the answer and named in `uploads.pending_upload_id`. When another mount uses that connection, or a request to the backend uses it meanwhile, the files keep uploading through it, and `uploads` says they are not delivered yet.
- `wait`: the same, and the answer waits up to `wait_seconds` (1 to 600, default 120) until nothing is held open and nothing is left to upload. `uploads.delivered` is then true. Otherwise it is false, with what was still held open and not uploaded (both null when uploads of the mount had already stopped with something left, now or before the DELETE, which is kept on the server), and the uploads go on as with `keep`; so they do when the client goes away while it waits. On a mount served by its backend's shared connection it waits for the connection, which the backend's other mounts write through too.
- `discard`: what is not uploaded yet is deleted now and is never uploaded, and so are the mount's uploads already kept on the server; files still open on the mount stop working, and `uploads.discarded` says how many files that was. On a mount that is already removed (by an earlier DELETE, one still waiting included) it is not refused: it deletes what the mount left in the same way, and answers 200 without `mount_path`. Refused for a mount served by its backend's shared connection (409 `UPLOADS_DISCARD_SHARED`).

Servers that take `uploads` list `mount_delete_uploads` in the `features` of GET /api/v1/version; an older server ignores it and keeps.

get.description: List unsent upload data. An item in state uploading holds files that are still being uploaded on their own, by uploads that kept running through a service restart or that belong to a mount that was removed or changed; stop it to hold them instead. An item in state pending holds files whose uploads stopped before they were sent (after a crash, a reboot or shutdown of the machine or computer, or a stop request): they may be incomplete or out of date. Each file keeps the reason it was held. Each item groups the files of one mount session, with a count per reason; list its files with GET /api/v1/pending-uploads/{id}/files. Nothing here expires: an item stays until every file is delivered, or it is discarded, so an item can show a delivery that covered only part of its files.

post.description: Upload held files of a pending upload to a backend. This overwrites newer versions of the same files on the backend, including changes made since the files were held back, so confirm with the owner of the data first, or download the files and compare. Without paths or paths_b64, every complete file is delivered; with them, only the files they name: paths takes listed paths, paths_b64 listed path_b64 values (the only way to name a file whose name is not valid UTF-8), and the two can be combined. A file named twice, or a name that is not one of the item's files, is refused with 400, and an incomplete file (complete: false) with 409; in both cases nothing starts. Incomplete files can only be downloaded or discarded. Without backend_id the item's saved connection settings are used; with backend_id, that backend's current settings are, and they become the item's saved settings once the upload starts (a delivery that fails before keeps the saved settings as they were; one cut short by a restart or an error while it switched them leaves them unsettled, listed in unsettled_backend_ids, and a delivery without backend_id is then refused with 409 until a delivery with backend_id switches them again); the files land at the same paths under it. While a delivery runs, the backend it uploads to cannot be updated, and deleting that backend with uploads=discard stops the delivery. The answer is 202 with the item in state delivering. Each file leaves the item as its upload lands. When the delivery ends, the item returns to pending with the files that were not delivered, and last_error says why when it ended early; the item disappears once no file is left, or when it is discarded. A delivery interrupted by a service restart, a crash, or a reboot or shutdown of the machine or computer returns the item to pending with its undelivered files; deliver it again.

get.description: Execute a JavaScript/TypeScript script based on hostname and path routing. Every HTTP method reaches the same script route, but behavior can depend on the method: a script that exports method-specific handlers runs the matching one, and HEAD falls back to GET. If no matching or catch-all handler exists, OPTIONS returns 204 and other methods return 405, with an Allow header. Other exceptions: OPTIONS is answered 204 by the CORS preflight before any script runs, unless a proxy hook dispatches it. A HEAD request runs the script but sends no body. PUT, PATCH and DELETE read a request body as POST does, and so does every other method except GET and HEAD when the request carries one (a Content-Length above 0 or a Transfer-Encoding), parsed by its Content-Type (JSON, form, multipart or raw bytes) unless the script declares `@rawBody`. A path ending in `.md` returns that documentation file instead of running a script, with or without a script beside it; beside a script it is served under that script's `@enabled` and `@token`. `/favicon.ico` is answered by the service itself (on an exclusive execId origin, one whose deployment directory holds an `.exclusive` marker, only that directory's own `favicon.ico` is served, else 404). When a proxy hook on this URL dispatches the request, OPTIONS, `.md` and `/favicon.ico` requests reach the hook script too, and it answers: `metadata.hook.forward()` relays the upstream's response; when the upstream cannot be reached, the hook script's `onUpstreamError` fallback answers, or the service answers 502 without a usable one. The hook's deadline answers 504, or closes the connection when the answer had already started. The script can answer with any status, Content-Type and body of its own; the statuses listed are the ones the service itself sends or falls back to.

200.description: The script's answer, or a documentation file. A script can set any status with `res.status()` and a Content-Type with `res.setHeader()`; without them the defaults below apply. A Content-Type the script set is kept for a returned object (other than an `Error`), string, stream (an async generator or `ReadableStream`) or other value; a returned `Response`'s own or detected Content-Type replaces it. A returned Buffer gets the type detected from its bytes, and a returned stream without a Content-Type gets `text/plain`. Headers the script already sent (`res.stream()`, `res.writeHead()`) stand. An object or array is sent as JSON. A string that starts, after leading whitespace, with `<!doctype html`, an HTML comment or an opening tag of a standard HTML element (`<h1>`, `<div class="x">`, `<svg>`) is sent as HTML. Any other string or value is sent as plain text, and a returned stream or async generator is written as it produces. A Buffer is sent with the type detected from its bytes. A returned `Response` is forwarded with its own status and headers, less the framing and hop-by-hop ones; one the script built without a Content-Type gets one from its first chunk when that chunk decodes as UTF-8: `application/json` when it starts as JSON, `text/html` when it starts as HTML (the rule a returned string gets), `text/plain` otherwise, an empty chunk included. With no such chunk (no body, a HEAD request, status 204 or 304, or a first chunk that is not UTF-8) none is added, and one the script set earlier stays. The rest of an answer whose headers the script already sent keeps them. A hook script's `metadata.hook.forward()` relays the upstream's status, headers and body, less the hop-by-hop ones; when the upstream cannot be reached, a synchronous `onUpstreamError` fallback that returns an object answers instead with the status it returns (502 unless it is an integer from 100 to 599), its headers less invalid and hop-by-hop ones, `text/plain` when it sets no Content-Type, an `X-Hoody-Hook-Audit` header, and its body when that is a string or Buffer (an empty body otherwise). A path ending in `.md` returns that documentation file instead of running a script; one beside a script is served under that script's `@enabled` and `@token`.

400.description: The service refused the request, the value the script returned, or the hoody-sdk in the scripts directory. A script can also answer with this status itself, with any body and Content-Type; the bodies below are the ones the service sends. The path is malformed: `Bad Request: URL path contains invalid percent-encoding.` or `Bad Request: URL path contains disallowed characters.` A proxy hook cannot send the client's own path to the upstream as written: it has a `.` or `..` segment (`%2e` forms included) or starts with `//`. `metadata.hook.forward()` answers so, and so does the service when `metadata.hook.fetchUpstream()` refused the path and the script then failed instead of answering. The body is `bad request path`, with `Cache-Control: no-store` and an `X-Hoody-Hook-Audit` header. The hostname is malformed: an HTML page headed `400 Bad Request` naming the problem. The script uses `@return-type-mode dev`, the service does not run in production, and the script returned a value that does not match its `@return-type`: `{"error": "Return type validation failed", "details": …, "expected": …, "actual": …}`. The same mismatch is a 500 in `strict` mode (the default) and in `dev` mode in production; `warn` mode only logs it and sends the value. The scripts directory holds a hoody-sdk from before the computer names, so the `hoody` global refused to build a client: no request was sent to any API. Upgrade the SDK in the scripts directory with the install command the message names (`npm i hoody-sdk@<version>`). The request's `Accept` names `application/json` and not `text/html`: the management API's error envelope, `{"error": <message>, "code": "upgrade_required", "details": {"code": "upgrade_required"}, "timestamp"}`. The same refusal to a request whose `Accept` does not ask for JSON: the sentence `VM Error in script '<name>': <message>` followed by ` (code upgrade_required)`.

Nothing matches this hostname and path, and the request's `Accept` names `application/json` and not `text/html`: the management API's error envelope, `{"error": "No script found for <path>", "code": "ERROR_404", "details": {"code": "SCRIPT_NOT_FOUND", …}, "timestamp"}`, with the same facts as the page, `tried` listing the script paths it tried in priority order and `suggestions` the routes near the path; when there is one, the `error` sentence ends `Did you mean <path>?` (several joined with ` or `). A matching script is disabled with `@enabled false`: `Not Found`. A `.md` path with no file, a system-prompt file (`<script>.system.md`, `_system.md`), or a file beside a disabled script: `Documentation not found: <path>`. A proxy hook dispatched the request and its target path has no script of its own (dynamic and catch-all routes and the index fallbacks never answer a hook): `hook target not found`, with `Cache-Control: no-store`.

get.description:
Streams new notifications as they are written.

- **WebSocket**: send a WebSocket upgrade request. A disallowed `Origin` (see `WS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`) is refused with `403` before the upgrade. Otherwise the server answers `101 Switching Protocols`; problems found after that arrive as JSON `error` frames on the socket, never as HTTP status codes: the per-IP connection limit (`WS_MAX_CONNECTIONS_PER_IP`) sends `error` and closes without a status code (clients see 1005); an invalid display ID in the query sends `error` and the socket stays open; too many client messages (`WS_MAX_MESSAGES_PER_MINUTE`, text and binary frames) sends `error` and closes with 1008. Close codes: 1000 server shutting down, 1001 heartbeat timeout (sent when a heartbeat tick finds the two earlier heartbeats unanswered by any client frame, pong included), 1008 message rate limit. A send that stalls for more than 10 seconds drops the connection without a close frame. Clients should reconnect with backoff after any close they did not start.
- **Server-Sent Events**: any other GET returns `200 text/event-stream`. Each event's `data` is one JSON message described in `x-async-api`; the first is `connected`. The `retry` field asks EventSource to reconnect after 3 seconds. The stream ends when the server shuts down.

Both transports send a `heartbeat` message (WebSocket: every `WS_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL` ms, first one interval after connect; SSE: every 15 seconds, first one right after `connected`) and a `resync` message when the client fell behind and notifications were skipped; re-fetch those with `GET /api/v1/notifications/{display}?since=<last seen timestamp>`.

`displays` is required for SSE. For WebSocket it is optional: without it no notification is delivered until the client sends a `subscribe` message. The protocol Ping and the `heartbeat` message are sent either way.

parameters.description: Comma-separated display IDs (`1,:2,3`), or `all` / `*` for every display. Required for SSE (400 without it). Optional for WebSocket: without it no notification is delivered until the client sends a `subscribe` message (Ping and `heartbeat` still arrive); an invalid ID arrives as an `error` frame after the upgrade.

get.description:
Retrieves notifications for one display, a comma-separated list of displays, or `all`.

Without `since`, `after_id` and `cursor` the response holds the newest `limit` notifications, newest first. With any of them it holds the OLDEST `limit` matching notifications after that point, oldest first, so a client can catch up page by page: pass `data.next_cursor` back as `cursor` while `data.has_more` is true, and the pages join into one ascending list with every matching notification exactly once. To read the whole history, start with `since=0`. Rows with the same timestamp, display and id (the same notification stored in two history files) are one notification and returned once.

Dismissed notifications are left out: a row is hidden when its id was dismissed globally or for its own display. Rows without an id are left out and do not count toward `limit`.

Without `username` or `session`, every history file is read (the same files the stream watches, including user session files), and only rows for the requested displays are returned. So any notification the stream delivered can be fetched again here, unless it was dismissed or has expired (`NOTIFICATION_TTL_MS`). `username`/`session` narrow the read to that user's (and session's) files: both -> `{username}-{session}-notifications.json`; `username` only -> that user's session files and `{username}-display-N` files; `session` only -> `*-{session}` files. Rows are still filtered by display.

parameters.description: A display ID (`1` or `:1`, up to 5 digits), a comma-separated list (`1,:2,3`), or `all`. Any invalid element rejects the whole request with 400.
parameters.name: display

parameters.description: Maximum number of notifications to return
parameters.name: limit

parameters.description: Forward start point, Unix milliseconds, inclusive: returns the oldest `limit` notifications with `timestamp >= since`, oldest first. Use it to start from a known time (`0` for the whole history); continue with `cursor` = `data.next_cursor`.
parameters.name: since

parameters.description: Forward cursor on notification id, exclusive: returns the oldest `limit` notifications with `id > after_id`, chosen and listed by id. Ids are numbered per display, so the filter is only meaningful for a single display; use `since` for lists and `all`. `data.next_cursor` of an `after_id` page continues in id order and keeps the request's `since` bound: with both `since` and `after_id`, every page reached by following it returns only rows with `timestamp >= since` and `id > after_id`.
parameters.name: after_id
cursor
parameters.description: Keyset cursor, exclusive: pass back `data.next_cursor` from an earlier response to get the oldest `limit` notifications after it, oldest first. The cursor keeps the order of the request that produced it: (timestamp, display, id), or id order (ties broken by timestamp, display) when that request used `after_id`. Rows that share a timestamp or id are never skipped or repeated. Opaque; cannot be combined with `since` or `after_id`.
Read only this user's history files (letters and digits only). See the operation description.
parameters.name: username

parameters.description: Read only this session's history files (letters and digits only). See the operation description.
parameters.name: session

displays.description: Displays the request covered: the string `"all"` for `/all`, otherwise the requested display IDs without the colon prefix or leading zeros, each listed once (`/0001,1` gives `["1"]`).

next_cursor.description: Forward position to continue from; pass it as `cursor`. On a page with `since`, `after_id` or `cursor` it is the last row in this page's selection order, which is also the last row listed. For a request with `after_id` (or a cursor from such a page) that order is id, ties broken by (timestamp, display), and the cursor keeps that order and the request's `since` bound. Otherwise the order is (timestamp, display, id). On a newest page (none of the three), listed newest first, it is the newest row, the first listed: following it returns only notifications stored later. An empty page returns the request's `cursor`, or `null` if none was sent. Following `next_cursor` until `has_more` is false returns every row the original request matched, each exactly once, and the pages join in that order.

has_more.description: `true` when more matching rows exist after `next_cursor` right now. Always `false` without `since`, `after_id` or `cursor` (the newest page).

400.description: Bad Request - invalid display list (any element), `limit` outside 1-1000, negative or non-numeric `since`/`after_id`, a `cursor` that is not a `next_cursor` from this endpoint or is combined with `since`/`after_id`, or a `username`/`session` with characters other than letters and digits. `error` is `Validation Error` and `details` names the parameter. The body has no `code` field.

invalid_display.summary: Display list is not numeric IDs or all

value.details: Display ID(s) must be numeric, optionally colon-prefixed, comma-separated if multiple, or "all".

value.error: Validation Error

value.details: "cursor" must be a next_cursor value returned by this endpoint

x-pagination.notes: Forward keyset paging. A request with none of `since`, `after_id` or `cursor` returns the newest page, newest first, with `has_more: false`; its `next_cursor` is the newest row, so following it returns only notifications stored later. To walk forward, start from `since` or `after_id` (or a stored `next_cursor`) and repeat with `cursor` = `data.next_cursor` while `data.has_more` is true. A walk that should cover the whole history and has no start point of its own sends `default_start` (`since=0`) on its first request. Every page of a walk is listed in the walk's order, oldest first: (timestamp, display, id), or id then (timestamp, display) after `after_id`. So the pages join into one ascending list holding every matching notification exactly once; rows with the same (timestamp, display, id) count as one notification. `next_cursor` is the last row listed, and it keeps the original `since`/`after_id` filters. There is no reverse cursor. `count` is the page length, never a total.

post.description:
Stores a browser push subscription so new notifications reach that device even with the page closed. Send the fields of `PushSubscription.toJSON()`. For use by the kit's notifications page: the browser's `Origin` header is required (https), and alert links open on that origin.

Posting an endpoint that is already stored refreshes it and returns its id (200). With `replacesEndpoint` (the browser rotated its subscription), the record of that endpoint takes the new one under the same id (200, `replaced: true`), so rotation never hits the limit; this applies only when the old record was created from the same origin. Otherwise a new record is created (201) unless `PUSH_MAX_SUBSCRIPTIONS` are stored (409).

Only endpoints of the browsers' push services are accepted (`PUSH_ALLOWED_ENDPOINT_HOSTS`).

get.summary: List the changes of a KV table
get.description:
Page through the changes made to a KV table, oldest first, or wait for the next ones (long poll). Every physical change of a row is one event, whoever made it (KV API, SQL through POST /db, another process): `set` (written), `ttl` (only the expiry changed), `delete`, `expire` (an expired row was removed). Changes are at-least-once and in order; events tell you what changed, so a client cache stays correct by applying them in order and re-reading values it needs (GET /kv/{key}/entry), or by asking for small values inline with include_values.

Start without `since`: the response has no events and `cursor` is the current position. To build a cache: take that cursor, then list the keys (GET /kv), then follow the changes from the cursor. Continue each page from `next_cursor`. `wait` (seconds) holds a request that has no events yet until one arrives or the time is up (capped one second before the request deadline; raise it with `timeout`); when the server shuts down, a waiting request answers at once with no events. `prefix` only returns keys starting with it; `next_cursor` still advances past other changes.

Cursors are opaque. 410 means the cursor cannot be continued: CHANGE_CURSOR_EXPIRED (older than the retained log, by default 24 hours or 1,000,000 changes per database) or CHANGE_CURSOR_INVALID (reason database_replaced: the file was replaced or restored, or reset_changes ran; table_changed: the table was dropped, renamed or changed outside the KV API; future_cursor). Re-read the state and start from a new cursor. Schema changes made outside the KV API (for example through POST /db) start a new table generation. Not available in directory mode.

parameters.name: db
parameters.description: Database path

parameters.name: table
parameters.description: KV table name (default: kv_store)

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: Cursor to continue after (next_cursor of the previous page, or the cursor of an event). Omit to get the current cursor.

parameters.name: prefix
parameters.description: Only keys starting with this prefix

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: Maximum events in the page (1-1000, default 100)

parameters.name: wait
parameters.description: Seconds to wait for the first event when there is none yet (0-60, default 0)

parameters.name: include_values
parameters.description: Attach the value to set/ttl events when it is still current, not expired and at most 256 KiB (otherwise value_omitted says why)

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Deadline for this request, in whole seconds, clamped to [1, 300]. Once it passes, a long operation stops at its next checkpoint rather than being cut off mid-step; a step already running, such as a filesystem scan or a wait for another writer, finishes first. A request that has not finished by then answers 503 REQUEST_TIMEOUT, except that a write which has already committed still returns its success. A value that is not a whole number is ignored and the default applies. This is a server-side deadline, not a client transport timeout. Omitted, the server default applies (30 seconds unless the deployment overrides it).

get.summary: Stream the changes of a KV table
get.description:
Server-Sent Events stream of the changes made to a KV table (see GET /changes for the events and cursors). Frames: `retry: 1000`, then `event: ready` (`id:` = the cursor the stream continues from, data `{"cursor","oldest_cursor"}`); `event: change` for each matching change (`id:` = its cursor, data = the event); `event: checkpoint` (`id:` = the position scanned, data `{"cursor"}`) every 15 s and after 1000 skipped changes, so a reconnect skips them; and, before the server closes the stream, `event: reset` (data `{"reason"}`: cursor_expired, database_replaced, table_changed, future_cursor. Re-read the state and start again) or `event: end` (data `{"reason"}`: database_deleted, shutdown, max_lifetime. Reconnect with the last id for shutdown and max_lifetime).

Resume with `Last-Event-ID` (the last `id:` received; wins over `since`). Without either, the stream starts at the current position. An invalid cursor at the start is a JSON 410 instead of a stream. A stream lasts at most one hour (server setting); the request timeout does not apply. The number of open streams is capped server-wide: over the cap the answer is 503 with Retry-After. Not available in directory mode.

post.description: Execute multiple SQL queries or statements in a single transaction with full ACID guarantees. Each item sends its SQL as `query` or `statement` (alias `sql`) and its bind values as `values` (alias `params`). A `statement` whose SQL produces result columns (SELECT, WITH, PRAGMA, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE ... RETURNING) returns its rows exactly like a `query`; one that produces none returns rowsUpdated. An unknown key on an item is refused with 400 UNKNOWN_FIELD, and `values` and `params` with different contents with 400 VALUES_CONFLICT. Foreign keys are enforced: REFERENCES constraints and their ON DELETE/ON UPDATE actions apply, and a violation is 409 SQL_CONSTRAINT. A request holding PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF runs with enforcement off as a whole, since SQLite cannot change the setting inside the transaction; the next request has it on again. PRAGMA defer_foreign_keys = ON instead defers the checks to the commit.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Deadline for this request, in whole seconds, clamped to [1, 300]. Once it passes, a long operation stops at its next checkpoint rather than being cut off mid-step; a step already running, such as a filesystem scan or a wait for another writer, finishes first. A request that has not finished by then answers 503 REQUEST_TIMEOUT, except that a write which has already committed still returns its success. A value that is not a whole number is ignored and the default applies. This is a server-side deadline, not a client transport timeout. Omitted, the server default applies (30 seconds unless the deployment overrides it).

get.description: Retrieve a value from the KV store with optional JSON path extraction and time-travel support. Without at_timestamp the body is the stored value itself, sent with its stored Content-Type (JSON when path is set). With a non-zero at_timestamp the body is always a JSON envelope carrying the value as it was at that time, and the X-Created-At, X-Updated-At and X-Expire-At headers are not sent.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key name (supports / for hierarchical keys)

parameters.name: db
parameters.description: Database file path or directory

parameters.name: table
parameters.description: Custom table name

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: JSON path for nested value extraction. The extracted value is returned as JSON with an X-JSON-Path header; a path that does not exist in the value answers 404. Ignored with at_timestamp.

parameters.name: at_timestamp
parameters.description: Unix timestamp. Returns the value the key held at that moment, in a JSON envelope instead of the current value. The value is reconstructed from the key's recorded history. When no recorded write establishes it, the current value is returned if it was already in place at that moment: with op_number 0 when the key has recorded history, and without op_number or op_timestamp when it has none (for example, a key written through SQL). A write made with history=false that leaves the value at that moment unknown answers 409 TIME_TRAVEL_CHAIN_GAP. 0 or omitted reads the current value; a time in the future is rejected with 400. A directory (directory mode) is rejected with 400 in this mode.

parameters.name: rebuild
parameters.description: Directory mode only: clear the directory's cached file information (this directory only, not its subdirectories), then read the key. Ignored with at_timestamp.

parameters.name: If-None-Match
parameters.description: Answers 304 while the key's current ETag matches.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Deadline for this request, in whole seconds, clamped to [1, 300]. Once it passes, a long operation stops at its next checkpoint rather than being cut off mid-step; a step already running, such as a filesystem scan or a wait for another writer, finishes first. A request that has not finished by then answers 503 REQUEST_TIMEOUT, except that a write which has already committed still returns its success. A value that is not a whole number is ignored and the default applies. This is a server-side deadline, not a client transport timeout. Omitted, the server default applies (30 seconds unless the deployment overrides it).

200.description: The stored value; with at_timestamp, a JSON envelope

ETag.description: The key's ETag; it changes on every write of the key, TTL changes included. Not sent with at_timestamp, in directory mode, or when the server could not verify the key's version

X-Created-At.description: Unix timestamp when created; in directory mode, the file modification time. Not sent with at_timestamp

X-Directory-Mode.description: Set to 'true' when db is a directory (directory mode)

X-Expire-At.description: Unix timestamp when the key expires; sent only when a TTL is set. Not sent with at_timestamp

X-File-Hash.description: SHA-256 of the value file, hex-encoded. Directory mode only, and not sent when path is set

X-JSON-Path.description: The path that was extracted, sent when path is set

X-KV-Nesting-Depth.description: Number of /-separated segments in the key. Directory mode only

X-KV-Reference.description: Set to 'true' if value is a KV store reference

X-Reference-Path.description: The reference target, sent with X-KV-Reference

X-Updated-At.description: Unix timestamp when last updated; in directory mode, the file modification time. Not sent with at_timestamp

schema.description: The stored value as raw bytes.
Without at_timestamp: the stored value, or with path the extracted value, as JSON of any type. With a non-zero at_timestamp: always the envelope object.

anyOf.description: The stored value as JSON. Any JSON type.

put.description: Store or update a value in the KV store with optional TTL, JSON path, and compare-and-swap. TTL and compare-and-swap are SQLite-mode features: a directory-mode store answers 400 to if_match, to an If-Match or If-None-Match header, and to a ttl above 0 (ttl=0 means no expiry and is accepted).

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key name

parameters.name: db
parameters.description: Database file path or directory

parameters.name: table
parameters.description: Custom table name

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: JSON path for nested value update

parameters.name: ttl
parameters.description: Time-to-live in seconds (SQLite mode only; a non-zero ttl against a directory-mode store is rejected with 400)

parameters.name: if_match
parameters.description: Compare-and-swap: write only if the key's current value equals this. Against a JSON value it is read as one JSON value and compared as a value: any spacing and key order, numbers as written (1 and 1.0 differ). Text that is not valid JSON is the string with that text, so v1 matches the stored string v1; a string whose text is itself JSON (such as 5 or true) is sent JSON-quoted. Against a text or binary value it compares byte for byte. SQLite mode only; rejected with 400 against a directory-mode store. Cannot be combined with an If-Match or If-None-Match header (400)

parameters.name: history
parameters.description: Store this write's value in history; false records only that the write happened, not what it wrote

parameters.name: create_db_if_missing
parameters.description: Create database file if it is missing. The legacy alias `auto_create` is still accepted and means the same thing; the two must agree when both are sent.

parameters.name: If-Match
parameters.description: Applies the write only if the key's current ETag matches.

parameters.name: If-None-Match
parameters.description: Set to * to write only if the key does not exist yet.

parameters.name: Idempotency-Key
parameters.description: Replays the stored response for a repeat of the same key. By default a receipt is kept for at most 24 h; the oldest are evicted early when the per-database receipt count or size budget is exceeded. The time and both budgets are configurable. After eviction a retry with the same key is applied again.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Deadline for this request, in whole seconds, clamped to [1, 300]. Once it passes, a long operation stops at its next checkpoint rather than being cut off mid-step; a step already running, such as a filesystem scan or a wait for another writer, finishes first. A request that has not finished by then answers 503 REQUEST_TIMEOUT, except that a write which has already committed still returns its success. A value that is not a whole number is ignored and the default applies. This is a server-side deadline, not a client transport timeout. Omitted, the server default applies (30 seconds unless the deployment overrides it).

get.description: Retrieve the operation history for a specific key showing all changes over time. Writes made with history=false appear as `UNRECORDED` entries: they record that an untracked write happened and the span of time it covers (`timestamp` to `unrecorded_until`), with no value, content type or expiry. They exist so time travel can answer "indeterminate" rather than a stale value once such a write's row is gone, and they count towards `limit`. A `SET` with `checkpoint: true` was recorded by a rollback, not a client: it keeps the value the rollback restored readable by time travel, and its old and new value are that same value. Operations are returned newest first (highest op_number first), so `limit` keeps the most recent ones.

post.description: Execute a command in the specified terminal session. Supports both local bash and remote SSH sessions. The terminal type is determined by URL parameters on first use. By default, if a DISPLAY is configured on the session, the endpoint waits for the Hoody Display to be ready before executing the command. The wait is skipped when no X server holds that display and none can be started (no xpra installed, or a display above 40000, and no startup script that could start it), since it could only time out. It can also be disabled with skip_display_wait=true. Use ephemeral=true for a guaranteed-unique isolated PTY session with no display/dbus and automatic cleanup, ideal for programmatic command execution (like a scripted command runner). On a local session the command is handed to the shell as a file, so any text runs as written (a `!`, an unbalanced quote or an open heredoc is the command's own business: bash reports a syntax error as exit code 2 and the session stays usable), and `stdout` holds only what the command printed (no prompt, banner or earlier output). On an SSH session the command is typed into the remote shell. With wait=true (the default) a local PTY command's response is normally the finished result (see wait), the same object GET /api/v1/terminal/result/{command_id} returns; with wait=false it returns at once with the command_id and status running (queued with defer_pid), and the result is polled from /result. The terminal is a PTY: stderr is merged into stdout, line endings are CRLF, escape sequences are removed and leading/trailing whitespace is trimmed. exit_code is the command's own exit status when `completion` is marker; see `completion` for the other cases. For the command's exact bytes use mode raw in the body: the command then runs as `bash -c` (`/bin/sh -c` when bash is not installed; `shell` in the response says which) in a process of its own, without a terminal and without a terminal session (terminal_id, ephemeral and the other session parameters are ignored; an SSH parameter is a 400). stdin is /dev/null or the decoded stdin_b64; stdout and stderr come back apart and unchanged in stdout_b64 and stderr_b64 (binary data, bare LF, whitespace, escape sequences), each up to the server's capture limit (the rest is read and dropped, with stdout_truncated / stderr_truncated set). The response is sent once the command has exited and stdout and stderr are closed, so a background process that keeps them open holds it until the timeout; redirect its output to let the command return. At the timeout, and when the client disconnects, the command's process group gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 3 s. A command started as another user through su, or through sudo with use_pty, runs in a session of its own, so a process there that ignores the SIGTERM it is passed can outlive this cleanup. Raw mode needs wait=true, and its command_id is not known to /result or /abort.

parameters.name: terminal_id
parameters.description: Terminal session ID (numeric; a new session needs 1-9999, an existing one up to 65535). Required unless ephemeral=true, in which case it is auto-generated if not provided. On calls routed through a terminal-N edge proxy hostname, the proxy sets this from the hostname label and OVERWRITES any value you send (a ?terminal_id=0 query sentinel never survives the proxy). Use the terminal-0 hostname as the "no terminal ID" sentinel so ephemeral=true can auto-generate; supply this parameter directly only when calling the terminal service without the proxy

parameters.name: ephemeral
parameters.description: When true, auto-generates a unique terminal_id (if not provided), skips display/dbus initialization, and applies aggressive cleanup. Designed for programmatic CLI command execution like a scripted command runner (default: false). WARNING: Do NOT use ephemeral=true for GUI applications that require a display. Ephemeral sessions strip the DISPLAY environment variable, which means X11/GUI applications will not work. Use a regular terminal session with an explicit terminal_id and display parameter instead for GUI workloads. A terminal_id that names a running terminal with a display is refused with 409 PERSISTENT_SESSION rather than turned ephemeral; on a terminal-N host the proxy sets terminal_id=N, so send ephemeral commands to the terminal-0 host

parameters.name: defer_pid
parameters.description: Defer command injection until this PID exits (TUI-safe). With defer_pid the response does not wait for completion even when wait=true (session setup and display readiness can still delay it)

parameters.name: defer_start_time_ticks
parameters.description: Optional /proc/<pid>/stat field 22 (starttime in clock ticks since boot) to avoid PID reuse bugs. If it mismatches, command executes immediately

parameters.name: defer_timeout_ms
parameters.description: Max time to wait for defer_pid exit before failing (default: 60000)

parameters.name: defer_poll_ms
parameters.description: Poll interval while waiting for defer_pid exit (default: 50, minimum: 10)

parameters.name: reset
parameters.description: Reset existing session and reconfigure (kills current process, clears state, allows switching from bash to SSH or changing any parameter) - Use 'true', '1', or no value

parameters.name: cwd
parameters.description: Working directory for local bash sessions (ignored for SSH). In raw mode: the command's working directory, when the body has no cwd

parameters.name: cwd_auto_create
parameters.description: Auto-create cwd when the requested working directory does not exist yet. Applies when cwd is explicitly provided for a new or reset local session, and to a command run with mode raw. Enable with 'true', '1', or no value (default: false)

parameters.name: shell

requestBody.description: Command execution parameters

command.description: The command to execute. In raw mode at most 131071 bytes

mode.description: pty (default): run in the terminal session and return cleaned terminal text. raw: run as a one-shot process on pipes and return the exact bytes in stdout_b64 and stderr_b64

stdin_b64.description: Raw mode only: base64 of the bytes to write to the command's stdin, which is then closed. Without it stdin is /dev/null

user.description: Raw mode only: system user to run the command as (default: the user query parameter, else the server's default user). Switching users goes through sudo -n, or su where sudo is not installed

id.description: Custom command ID (numeric 1-65535, auto-generated if not provided). Ignored in raw mode

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds, from 0 to 2000000. A fraction is rounded up to whole seconds (0.5 becomes 1 second); a negative value is refused with 400 INVALID_TIMEOUT. 0 or omitted means no timeout on a persistent session and 600 seconds on an ephemeral one. In PTY mode it starts when the command is submitted for execution, once any display, defer_pid or SSH readiness wait is over; for a local command queued behind an earlier one on the same session the time in the queue counts, and a command still waiting when it elapses is never run. When it elapses the result is status timed_out with exit_code 124; on a persistent session a command that was running keeps running in the shell (commands behind it wait until it has finished); on an ephemeral one the command's job and the shell get SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 3 s. In raw mode 0 or omitted means the server's default (600 seconds); at the timeout the command's process group gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 3 s, and the result is status timed_out with completion timeout. A command started as another user through su, or through sudo with use_pty, runs in a session of its own, so a process there that ignores the SIGTERM it is passed can outlive this cleanup

wait.description: Whether to wait for completion (default: true). For PTY commands only a local session waits: an SSH session and a request with defer_pid return at once, and a local request also returns at once when 256 other requests are already waiting for their commands. Check `status` in the response and poll GET /api/v1/terminal/result/{command_id} when it is not final. Raw mode refuses false

cwd.description: Working directory for command execution (for local bash only). The session stays in that directory afterwards

require_staged.description: Run the command only from a staged file for the shell's user, never typed into the terminal. When it cannot be staged (an SSH session, a user the server cannot write files for), the answer is 409 STAGING_UNAVAILABLE and nothing runs. Not with mode raw

track.description: Tracked execution: needs require_staged, incarnation and id, implies wait=false (omit wait or send false: wait=true is refused with 400 VALIDATION_ERROR) and refuses timeout, reset, ephemeral, defer_pid and mode raw. The command runs only after the server lets its starter go, in a process group of its own made the terminal's foreground group; every process it starts stays a member until it exits. Read the workload with GET /api/v1/terminal/workloads and signal it with POST /api/v1/terminal/workloads/{command_id}/signal. Env values travel only in a staged file that is removed when the command starts, never in the terminal, its history or any answer. Sending the same incarnation, id, command, cwd, env and track_label again answers 200 with replayed true and runs nothing, also when both requests waited for the display together and when the terminal's command backlog is full; a different command under the same pair answers 409 COMMAND_ID_EXISTS

incarnation.description: The incarnation of the terminal's shell (from create or GET /api/v1/terminal/sessions): the command is admitted only on that shell, else 409 INCARNATION_MISMATCH. Required with track

track_label.description: With track: a label kept on the workload, 1 to 64 characters of a-z, 0-9, colon and hyphen; omit it for no label

env.description: Environment variables for this command only, as string values. On a local session they do not persist into later commands, also after an abort, and a shadowed variable gets its earlier value back (on bash with its attributes) (a cd or export done by the command itself does persist). Keys must be shell variable names ([A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*) not starting with __HOODY_ (any case), else 400. On an SSH session they are exported in the remote shell and persist

servers.description: The computer's terminal kit: projectId and computerId name the computer, server the server that hosts it, and serviceIndex the kit instance (1-9999).

post.description: Create a new terminal session or return success if it already exists (code already_active; the session keeps the configuration it was created with). A running ephemeral session is not returned for a request that does not ask for one: that is 409 EPHEMERAL_SESSION. By default, when a Hoody Display is configured, the endpoint blocks until the display server is accepting connections. This ensures the caller can immediately use the display after the response.

parameters.description: Terminal session ID. On a terminal-N edge proxy hostname the proxy sets it to N; a different terminal_id in the body is refused with 400 TERMINAL_ID_MISMATCH. Terminal 0 (the terminal-0 hostname) only starts an ephemeral session with a generated id.

ephemeral.description: Enable ephemeral session mode. A terminal id in 5001-7999 is generated when the body gives none and the query gives none or gives terminal_id=0. Ephemeral sessions are cleaned up after an idle timeout and have DISPLAY removed. (default: false)

get.description: Retrieve the current or final results of a command execution. Can be called while command is running or after completion. On a terminal-N edge proxy hostname the command must belong to terminal N (the proxy sets the request's terminal_id from the hostname label): a command of another terminal is answered 404 COMMAND_NOT_FOUND, the same as an id that does not exist. The terminal-0 hostname reaches the commands of ephemeral sessions (the ones started with ephemeral=true) and no others, so a command started there is read and aborted there. A direct request without a terminal_id reaches any command.

delete.description: Completely destroy and remove a terminal session. This ends the session's shell, frees its resources and removes the session. For an ephemeral session only the shell is signalled, so background processes it started can keep running. Running tracked workloads keep running. Attached WebSocket clients are closed with code 4410 and reason `session deleted`, a code hoody-sdk and the web client do not reconnect on by themselves: an attach creates the session it names, so a reconnect would start a fresh shell under the deleted id. Use this to cleanly terminate sessions without waiting for idle timeout. A display the session started (its `display`, desktop environment included) is not part of the session: it keeps running for other sessions and Hoody Display. A GUI program started from the session's own shell is part of the session and ends with it unless it detached (setsid, nohup). Stop the display with `POST /api/v1/system/displays/{display}/stop`.

post.summary: Freeze (SIGSTOP) a process or process tree
post.description: Suspend execution of one or more processes by delivering `SIGSTOP`. The kernel halts every thread of the target's thread group until a matching `SIGCONT` is delivered (see `/api/v1/system/processes/unfreeze`). Target by PID or by process name; optionally fan out across all descendants via a one-shot `/proc` PPID snapshot. Use this for pausing background workloads (builds, fine-tunes, AI inference) without losing in-memory state. Permission is enforced by the kernel: non-root callers can only freeze their own UID's processes (`EPERM` otherwise).

A guarded PID reached through `name` or `include_descendants` is not signalled: it is listed in `skipped` with error GUARDED and the request still returns 200

post.description: Cancel a command that was started via the execute endpoint. Graceful mode (default) sends SIGINT via the PTY (equivalent to Ctrl+C). Force mode sends SIGKILL to the process group. Partial output captured before abort is preserved in the response. A command still waiting for an earlier one on its session (or for defer_pid) is cancelled without sending anything; it never runs. A command that hit its timeout, or whose wait ended with completion output_quiet, keeps running in the shell, so it can still be aborted as long as nothing else has reached that terminal since it was sent (no other command, keystrokes, write, press or paste, nor typing through a pid attachment into any terminal on this server, which cannot be told apart) and its shell is still the same running process; the result then shows status cancelled; timed_out stays true for a command that hit its timeout and stays false for one whose wait ended with output_quiet. Idempotent: aborting a command that already finished or was already aborted, or a timed-out command after other input reached its terminal, returns 409 with the existing result and sends nothing. Known limitation: graceful abort may not stop processes that trap SIGINT. Use force=true for those. On a terminal-N edge proxy hostname the command must belong to terminal N (the proxy sets the request's terminal_id from the hostname label): a command of another terminal is answered 404 COMMAND_NOT_FOUND, the same as an id that does not exist. The terminal-0 hostname reaches the commands of ephemeral sessions (the ones started with ephemeral=true) and no others, so a command started there is polled and aborted there. A direct request without a terminal_id reaches any command.

get.description: Returns a JSON array of the terminal sessions with session metadata and recent command history (best-effort), followed by the terminals of hoody-daemon programs that are not open yet. A program's terminal (a daemon program configured with terminal_id, or the socket of a quick-start program, listed with running false once its launcher is gone) has daemon_program true, shell null, no command history, pid set to the program's session leader while connected, is_active true while hoody-terminal is connected to the running program, display_id from the program's configuration, and a daemon object: program_id, program_name, user and enabled from the program's configuration (null for a quick-start program), running (its launcher is listening), connected (hoody-terminal is attached to it) and ended (it ended while attached). Every other session has daemon_program false; its daemon object is null unless a daemon program claims the same id (a local session that predates the program, which blocks attaching to it until deleted). cols and rows are the terminal's current size (attached clients and snapshots use it), null until a client or an API call has sized it; a program started by an older hoody-daemon, which does not record its session, is not resized to it. A local session with a running shell also has incarnation (32 lowercase hex characters, new for every shell the session starts), user and uid (the account and effective uid its shell runs as); they are null for daemon programs and sessions without a shell; user and uid can also be null when the identity cannot be determined.

post.description: Stop the X display :{display} and everything drawing on it. A display started by a terminal session (the session's `display`, with or without `desktop`/`desktop_env`) keeps running when that session is deleted, desktop environment included, so it stays usable from other sessions and from Hoody Display; this route is how it ends. The display's session server gets SIGTERM, which shuts down its X server (a session server that exits while still starting up can leave its X server running; that X server then gets SIGTERM too); the window manager, panels and applications on the display exit with it. A display without a session server has its X server signalled directly. Whatever is still running after 10 seconds gets SIGKILL (`forced` true). A Hoody Display screenshot of the display that is in progress is waited for first (up to 25 seconds; then the stop is refused with DISPLAY_BUSY and nothing is signalled). The response is sent once the display is gone. Only displays the terminal service can reach are found, so an X server you started with `-nolisten local` is not found. Background services a desktop started outside the display (for example a D-Bus session bus) are not stopped. Sessions whose `DISPLAY` points at the stopped display keep running; the next session created with that display starts it again.

get.description: Returns a rendered snapshot of the terminal screen. The response includes the visible text grid (lines array), cursor position, window title, fullscreen (alt-screen) state, reverse-video highlight spans, and a monotonic sequence counter. Optionally includes ANSI SGR colored lines. The snapshot is built from a server-side terminal emulator that follows the browser's xterm.js state, with one difference: a row that starts with one of the command markers that /api/v1/terminal/execute writes is returned as an empty string, and /find and /wait search it as a blank row, so the browser can show a line that the snapshot leaves blank. get.description: Search the rendered terminal screen (or scrollback) for a PCRE2 regular expression pattern. Returns cell-coordinate hits with matched text. Supports case-insensitive matching, result limits, and scope selection (screen, scrollback, or all). Pattern length is capped at 1024 bytes. Match limits are enforced to prevent ReDoS. Rows are searched one at a time, and a row ends after its last non-blank cell plus one blank cell, so a pattern anchored at the row end matches the prompt users see: `>>> $` matches a Python prompt and `\$ $` a shell prompt, although the row is padded with blank cells to the terminal width. Hits on the full padded row are kept too (`>>>[ ]+$` still reports the whole run of blanks); a hit made only of padding at the padded edge, such as `$` at the last column, is replaced by the same row end at the visible end, so a row end is reported once. `col` and `length` count cells (a wide character is 2). `\C` (match one byte) is refused as an invalid regex (400 INVALID_REGEX), here and in `/wait`, because it could split a UTF-8 character.

The `deadline_exceeded` flag is `true` when the scan hit the internal 500 ms wall-clock bound (ReDoS-shaped patterns); `truncated` is `true` when `total >= limit`. When the regex engine gives up on a row (match limit, depth limit or out of memory), that row is not evaluated and the response also carries `search_error: true` and `search_error_code`; `hits` then holds only the matches in the other rows, so an empty `hits` does not mean the pattern matches nothing. post.description: Block until a terminal condition is met, then return an atomic snapshot of the screen at the moment of resolution. Supports three modes: stable (no screen updates for debounce_ms), regex (PCRE2 pattern matches on screen), or either (first condition wins). The regex search is the one `/find` uses, with the same row-end rule: `>>> $` matches a prompt although its row is padded with blank cells. A regex wait resolves at once on a match already on screen; to wait for the next prompt instead, send `fresh: true` (only rows changed after the wait starts can match) or `after_seq` (only rows changed after that `seq`, taken from `snapshot.seq` of `/snapshot` or of the previous `/wait`). A row that only scrolled keeps its age; a resize or leaving the alternate screen makes every row count as changed. The response includes a full snapshot for the matched/stable/timeout/exited terminal statuses so clients avoid a TOCTOU race between wait and a follow-up /snapshot call; the vterm_reinit status is the lone exception: it fires when the terminal emulator was torn down mid-wait and no coherent snapshot can be captured (client should retry). By default a session allows 16 concurrent waiters; `wait_max_waiters_per_session` in GET /api/v1/terminal/automation/metrics gives the limit that applies.

Fix the pattern rather than retrying: the failure is deterministic). With `after_seq` or `fresh` the response also carries `after_seq`, the seq the regex leg searched after.

get.description: Establishes WebSocket connection for real-time bidirectional terminal I/O. Multiple clients can share the same terminal session using the same terminal_id; a client that omits terminal_id joins the shared terminal "1" unless it asks for ephemeral=true. Request the `tty` subprotocol. The protocol uses binary framing where the first byte indicates message type. After the upgrade the client MUST send the JSON_DATA handshake frame (the JSON object itself, starting with '{', carrying columns and rows); the server spawns the session's process only once that frame arrives, so a client that never sends it gets no shell. Resizing is WebSocket-only (the RESIZE_TERMINAL frame); there is no REST resize. The session-creation parameters (everything except terminal_id, readonly, reset and cmd; see cmd) take effect only when this connection creates the session; joining a session that is already running ignores them. Supports session sharing, read-only mode, SSH connections, PID attachment, and comprehensive terminal features. A terminal_id that belongs to a hoody-daemon program (a program configured with terminal_id) attaches to that program's terminal: every client sees its screen and writable clients type into it, the program gets the smallest size among the writable clients (read-only clients count only when none is writable), and the session-creation parameters, cmd and pid are ignored. Such a connection is closed with code 4404 and reason `daemon program not running` when the program is not running, with 4404 and `daemon program ended` when it ends while attached (a later attach reaches a restarted program), and with 4409 when a local session already holds the id.

Omitted, the connection joins the shared terminal "1" that every client without a terminal_id uses; with ephemeral=true it instead gets a fresh ID in 5001-7999, reported in the SET_TERMINAL_ID frame. A value that is present but malformed is refused, never mapped to "1". 0 (the terminal-0 host) only starts a fresh ephemeral session: without ephemeral=true (or in agent mode) the connection is refused, never mapped to "1". Multiple clients can share by using the same ID. On connections routed through a terminal-N edge proxy hostname, the proxy sets this from the hostname label and overwrites any value you send. On a terminal-N edge proxy hostname, N must be at most 9999 and outside the numbers reserved for agent sessions; an existing id above that range (up to 65535) is reached only without the proxy.

patch.description: Reconfigure a live watcher in place. Omitted fields keep their current values. The watcher keeps its id, its replay history and its connected SSE/WebSocket clients; only the file-system backend is replaced. Reconfiguration preserves replay history, except that lowering `history_size` evicts retained events beyond the new capacity (minimum 32). Later replay returns 409 `HISTORY_GAP` if an event strictly after the requested cursor was evicted or could not be retained; `since_id=0` always returns retained history without a gap. The new backend starts before the old one stops, and events the old backend had already queued are processed before the handoff completes. So a change under a path watched by both configurations is not lost across the swap (one landing inside that window may be reported twice), and a change under a path only the old configuration watched is delivered if the old backend saw it before stopping. The drain is bounded: if the old backend has not finished within 5 seconds (a backstop against a wedged backend), the handoff completes anyway and events still queued in the old backend at that point are dropped, with a warning in the service log. A request that fails leaves the watcher unchanged. A body with no field is refused with 400 `INVALID_REQUEST`; a body whose fields all equal the current values returns the watcher as it is, without replacing the backend.

parameters.description:
Page number (1-based), counted from the oldest event still retained.
History is a ring buffer: if events are evicted between two page
requests the offsets shift and a page walk can skip events without an
error. Walk with `after_id` instead to have that reported. Without

parameters.name: after_id
parameters.description:
Continue a walk: return the `limit` events after this event id (the
previous response's `next_after_id`, a decimal event id; a typed client
passes it as a number). `since_id`, `since_timestamp`
and `page` are ignored when it is set. `since_timestamp` is then not
checked, but `since_id` and `page` must still be non-negative whole
numbers: any other value is refused with 400 (`INVALID_CURSOR` for
`since_id`, `INVALID_PAGINATION` for `page`). If any event after it has been
evicted from history since, the request fails with `409 HISTORY_GAP`
rather than skipping it.

get.description: Live events about the crontabs of the computer's users: managed entries created, updated or deleted (`source` api, expired or external), whole crontabs replaced or edited (`crontab_changed`, sent after the entry events of that change), and runs of managed jobs (`job_started`, `job_finished`). Edits made outside this service, such as `crontab -e` or `crontab -r`, appear within about 2 seconds with `source: external`. Job events come from the crontab line of an enabled managed entry, which reports its own start and end: scheduled runs of raw lines (lines this service did not write) and of entries in a crontab whose `SHELL` is not a POSIX shell are not reported; Run now of a managed entry is always recorded and sends job events; and a job whose shell exits without reporting its end (it replaced itself with `exec`, or was killed) finishes with `outcome: lost`. Events are kept in memory only: the history used by `since_id` (the last 1024 events by default) is lost when the service restarts, and a `since_id` from before a restart answers 409 `HISTORY_GAP`. Runs are also kept on disk (GET /api/v1/cron/runs), so after a restart read them there (only the runs that reached the disk: see that operation).

get.description: Live events about the crontabs of the computer's users: managed entries created, updated or deleted (`source` api, expired or external), whole crontabs replaced or edited (`crontab_changed`, sent after the entry events of that change), and runs of managed jobs (`job_started`, `job_finished`). Edits made outside this service, such as `crontab -e` or `crontab -r`, appear within about 2 seconds with `source: external`. Job events come from the crontab line of an enabled managed entry, which reports its own start and end: scheduled runs of raw lines (lines this service did not write) and of entries in a crontab whose `SHELL` is not a POSIX shell are not reported; Run now of a managed entry is always recorded and sends job events; and a job whose shell exits without reporting its end (it replaced itself with `exec`, or was killed) finishes with `outcome: lost`. Events are kept in memory only: the history used by `since_id` (the last 1024 events by default) is lost when the service restarts, and a `since_id` from before a restart answers 409 `HISTORY_GAP`. Runs are also kept on disk (GET /api/v1/cron/runs), so after a restart read them there (only the runs that reached the disk: see that operation).

101.description: WebSocket upgraded. The server sends one JSON text frame per event, with its `type`. A `lag` frame means the client fell behind the retained history and is followed by close code 4409. When the service stops it sends `{"type":"end","reason":"shutdown"}` and closes with 1012; reconnect later with since_id. Frames the client sends are ignored. The server pings every 20 s and closes a peer that misses a pong.

get.description: The latest runs of managed jobs, newest first, from the reports the jobs' crontab lines send (see the event stream). The service keeps the runs still running (a scheduled job that starts while 500 runs, scheduled and Run now together, are already running still runs but is not listed; Run now has its own limit of 16 simultaneous runs by default) and, for each entry, its last 50 ended runs of the last 30 days, at most 10 000 ended runs in all, in a history file capped at 5 MiB (the oldest ended runs are dropped first). They are kept on disk, so a restart keeps them: a run still running at the restart is followed again, or recorded `lost` when its shell is gone. When the disk cannot be used, or a write fails later, runs from then on are kept in memory only and a restart loses them; runs that reached the disk before stay (`GET /api/v1/cron/info` `history_persisted` says which). Page back with `before` (the `started_at` of the last run received). Raw lines and entries in a crontab whose `SHELL` is not a POSIX shell have no scheduled runs listed; Run now runs are listed.

get.description:
Returns plain text usage instructions showing how to send and receive data using curl. The help text includes the server's own URL (derived from Host header) so examples can be copied and run directly.

**Sections:** receiving data, sending files/text/directories with `curl -T`, `?download` and `?filename` control, `?video` browser playback, `?progress` transfer monitoring, end-to-end encryption with OpenSSL.

Also accessible at `/help`.

get.description:
Returns the standardized 9-field health response. Unauthenticated. Only
reachable at `/api/v1/pipe/health`. A bare `/health` returns 404 with the body `[ERROR] '/health' is not a valid path. Use '/api/v1/pipe/health'.\n`. Both are matched like reserved paths (case-insensitive, one trailing `/` or `.` allowed), so `/api/v1/pipe/health/` also returns this JSON and `/Health` also returns 404. Methods other than GET/HEAD/OPTIONS return 405 with `[ERROR] Method <verb> is not allowed.\n` and `Allow: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS`.
