directory.description: Working directory for the program (defaults to user home directory if not specified)

priority.description: Start priority: programs with lower numbers start first. No range is enforced.

stdout_logfile.description: Path to standard output log file

stderr_logfile.description: Path to standard error log file

logs_enabled.description: Whether logging is enabled for this program. Default: true.

log_max_bytes.description: Maximum size of each log file in bytes before rotation. Default: 5242880 (5MB).

log_backups.description: Number of rotated backup log files to keep. Default: 2.

hoody_kit.description: Indicates if this is a Hoody Kit program: its directory is under /hoody/plugins, or it carries an official kit name and its executable is under /hoody/plugins. Server-derived from the program's directory, name and command; not settable via the API.

inject_computer_env.description: Whether the daemon adds the computer's environment (PID 1's) to the program's. When absent: true for a Hoody Kit program (see `hoody_kit`), false for every other program. When true, the daemon's injection mode applies: by default a Kit program gets only the `HOODY_*` variables and any other program all of them; `--inject-all-env` and `--inject-hoody-env-only` override that for every program. When false, nothing from PID 1 is added, `HOODY_*` included, except the variables the program's `command` names as `$X`, `${X}` or `%(ENV_X)s`: each of those is resolved from the program's `environment`, then PID 1, then (for `$X` and `${X}` in a program without `port_range`) the daemon's own environment, and only that variable is added. A named variable is filtered like any other source: for a sandboxed program a value that is not literal, or a loader name, is dropped; a named variable with no value anywhere is left alone. This controls the daemon's own injection only: the program still inherits the environment of the process manager that runs it. Absent from the response when it was never set.

boot_if_exists.description: Absolute path of a marker file. Every time the daemon starts, it starts this program once if the path is a regular file (a symlink, a directory or a missing path does not count) and the process manager has not started the program since it came up. A program that is running stays as it is, and one that was stopped by hand stays stopped on a daemon restart or an update, but a reset stops and removes every program and replays the defaults, so after a reset a program whose file exists is started even if it had been stopped by hand; when the file is absent the program stays lazy. Meant for a lazy program (`lazy_load`) that must be running after a reboot only while it has work: the program keeps the file present while it does. The path must be absolute, contain no `..` segment and no control character, and be at most 4096 bytes. Allowed only for a standard program or a `port_range` of a single port (`start` equal to `end`); a wider range is refused with 400, on create and on an edit that widens the range of a program that has it. The daemon looks at the file only while it starts, never afterwards, so setting this field on an existing program starts nothing by itself. It does not change `boot` or `lazy_load`. Absent from the response when it was never set.

port_range.description: Port range for multi-instance programs. Defines a range of ports where each port creates a separate INSTANCE (actual running process). Example: ports 8000-8099 creates 100 potential instances. Each instance runs the same command with a different --port argument. Can be combined with lazy_load for on-demand startup. A range must not overlap any other stored program's range. When either side has an effective sandbox, its ports are also compared with enabled programs' declared listening sets, and ports held by active or draining sandbox firewall records are refused until those records are gone. On edit the object replaces the stored range and needs both `start` and `end`.

end.description: Inclusive ending port, at least `start`. Both endpoints are 1 to 65535, and `end - start + 1` must not exceed 4096.

port_param.description: Parameter name to pass port to command. Valid ONLY together with port_range; sending it on its own is rejected with "port_param requires port_range to be set". Has no schema default on purpose. Omit it and the server applies --port itself, so a default here would make every port-less create fail.

lazy_load.description: Enable lazy loading. When true, program/instances NOT started automatically. Started on-demand by edge proxy via ensure-started endpoint. Cannot be combined with boot:true.

ready_port.description: TCP readiness port (lazy mode). When set, a start with wait=true succeeds only once this port accepts a TCP connection and the program is up: it is reported running, or it is still starting and only its own processes listen on this port. For standard programs whose port lives in their own command line (hoody-agent :45). The port counts as ready once the program accepts the TCP connection the daemon opens to it from inside the computer; a program that does not accept that connection never becomes ready (each attempt waits up to 300 ms). An accepted connection shows that something listens on that port, not that it is this program's listener or that it serves anything. `0` is refused. It is checked against active or draining sandbox firewall reservations, and against enabled programs' declared listening sets when either side has an effective sandbox; two unsandboxed programs' readiness ports are not compared. With `if_not_running`, an already-running or shared result can come back without this polling, and an already-running port-range instance is not probed.

stop_wait_seconds.description: Seconds a stop waits for the program to exit after the stop signal before it is killed. Absent: 10 seconds.

display.description: X11 DISPLAY number for GUI programs. Accepts both "1" and ":1" formats (auto-prepends ":" if missing). Sets the DISPLAY environment variable for the program.

terminal_id.description: Hoody Terminal integration: Session ID (1-65535). Designed for use with hoody-terminal web interface. When specified, program runs in that terminal: terminal N of the computer, opened at the `terminal-N` host in a browser, with `hoody daemon programs terminal connect`, or with the SDK's `client.daemon.programs.connectTerminal`. The program's input and output are connected to that terminal session. The program runs as its `user`, root or not, and gets `TERM=xterm-256color` unless its environment sets `TERM`. When the command ends, the program ends with the command's exit code, so its status and `autorestart` follow the command, and clients attached to its terminal are disconnected with WebSocket close code 4404 (`daemon program ended`); a restarted program is reached by attaching again. In interactive mode that is when the shell left after the command ends, and with `tmux` when the tmux client does. Output the program writes while hoody-terminal has no connection to it waits in the terminal, up to about 19 KB, and a program that writes more blocks until something attaches; once anything has attached or used the terminal's REST automation, hoody-terminal stays connected until the program ends or the terminal session is deleted. Output that reaches hoody-terminal, the program's stderr included, is also written to the program's stdout log as raw terminal output (control sequences and `\r\n` line ends kept), with the same size limit and rotation as any program's log, so its last output can still be read with the program's logs after it ends, when its terminal no longer answers. Two kinds of output are not in that log: output still waiting in the terminal when the program ends because nothing had attached, and output written faster than the log takes it in. The stderr log holds errors from setting up the terminal and from its connections; warnings are left out. A stop ends everything the program runs in its terminal: TERM first, KILL after 7 s for whatever ignores it.

terminal_shell.description: Hoody Terminal integration: the shell that loads the environment, or `tmux`. A non-blank value requires `terminal_id`, and the daemon accepts only an installed `bash`, `zsh`, `fish`, `sh` or `tmux`. A blank string means direct execution, like an omitted one. With a shell, the command is one shell command line (pipes, `&&` and variables work); without one, its words are passed as they are, with quotes grouping words and nothing expanded, and, as for a program without a terminal, a `#` or `;` after a space starts a comment, even inside quotes. Omit it, or send null, for direct execution.

terminal_interactive.description: Hoody Terminal integration: Override auto-detection of interactive vs service mode. true = force interactive mode (-ic, shell persists after command exits), false = force service mode (-c, exec replaces shell), undefined/null = auto-detect based on command (recommended). Auto-detection recognizes 25+ AI coding assistants, editors, shells, multiplexers, and REPLs. In service mode the shell loads its rc file and is replaced by the command when it is a single command; a list, pipe or leading assignment runs as written. In interactive mode the command runs and the shell stays.

webhooks.description: Webhook notification configuration for real-time program lifecycle events (start, stop, crash, etc.) `enabled` and `urls` are REQUIRED whenever this object is present: the daemon's `WebhookConfig` has no default for either, so a webhooks object without them is a 400 from the add or edit handler (`invalid program body: missing field ...`). On an edit the two are replaced rather than merged, and only `events`, `headers`, `timeout` and `retry` keep their stored value when omitted, so a partial webhook edit has to resend `enabled` and `urls`. `webhooks: null` does not clear stored webhooks. Delivery needs more than this object: the daemon's `notifications.enabled` and `notifications.event_listener_enabled` must be true and the daemon's event listener must be running. Known limitation: event-driven delivery is not verified end to end; poll status for monitoring that has to be reliable.

enabled.description: Enable webhooks for this program

urls.description: Webhook URLs. When `enabled` is true: 1 to 5 URLs, HTTPS, no credentials, and public destinations only. A disabled configuration skips these checks. A name that resolves to a non-public address can save and then fail at delivery.

events.description: A single event name or an array, trimmed and case-insensitive: `STARTING`, `RUNNING`, `BACKOFF`, `STOPPING`, `STOPPED`, `EXITED`, `FATAL`, `UNKNOWN` (without `PROCESS_STATE_`). `[]`, `"all"` or `"*"` select all, and a new configuration without `events` selects all. On edit, omitted `events` keep the stored filter.

headers.description: Custom HTTP headers, at most 10 when `enabled` is true. On edit, supplied headers replace the stored map and omitted headers keep it.

timeout.description: Request timeout in seconds. When `enabled` is true it must be 1 to 60; when no value is stored the dispatcher uses 10.

retry.description: Retry attempts on failure. When `enabled` is true it must be 0 to 5; when no value is stored the dispatcher uses 3.

sandbox.description: Per-program confinement. Returned as stored: the submitted values, with optional fields that were left null omitted; a submitted block that restricts nothing is stored as absent and does not appear here. Absent means the program runs unconfined, as it does today.

status.description: Runtime status of the program. Present when include_status=true, or when include_stats=true and include_status is not given (include_stats implies include_status). Exactly one shape applies: standard programs carry `id`/`status`, port-range programs carry `type: "port-range"` plus instance counts.

stats.description: Resource stats (CPU, memory, process tree) for the program. Only present when include_stats=true and the program is running. For port-range programs, stats appear per-instance inside the status.instances array.

daemon_Program.description: `command`, `environment`, `directory`, `user`, `webhooks`, `sandbox` and the log paths can be left out of a list response; a client must not rely on them being present there.

id.description: Specific id to assign, 0 to 2147483646 (optional; auto-assigned when omitted).

name.description: Program name. Must be unique, start with a letter or digit, and contain only letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_`, up to 128 characters.

command.description: Command to execute with full arguments for your custom program. Use only for custom applications/scripts; system services (`apache2`, `nginx`, `mysql`, etc.) belong under `systemctl`. Must not contain a line feed, carriage return or NUL.

user.description: System user (must exist on the system). A Linux account name matched case-insensitively: starts with a letter or `_`, continues with letters, digits, `_` and `-`, may end in `$`, at most 32 bytes. A sandboxed program cannot run as an account resolving to uid 0.

enabled.description: Enable the program immediately

boot.description: Start automatically on system boot. A program with a `display` is started as soon as that display is ready.

delay_seconds.description: The startup window: seconds the program must STAY RUNNING for the start to count as successful. Nothing is postponed: the program is launched immediately. NOTE that 0 does NOT disable the window: at 0 the window is 1 second. Under `autorestart` `"unexpected"` or `"true"`, a non-zero exit or a signal inside the window is a FAILED start, retried a limited number of times and then marked `fatal`. An end that is not a crash under `autorestart` (any end under `"false"`, an exit 0 otherwise) is not a failed start, however quick: the daemon holds it back until the window has passed, so a one-shot runs once. Under `"false"` and `"unexpected"` it is reported as `exited` as soon as it ends, with its exit code or its signal in `last_run`; under `"true"` it is not reported as `exited` and is started again once the window has passed. A stop, edit or removal sent in that window can take up to this long to return. Hoody Kit programs keep the plain rule: the window is also 1 second at 0, and any exit inside the window is a failed start, whatever `autorestart` says.

autorestart.description: Restart policy: `"unexpected"` (default) restarts after an exit code other than 0, including a deliberate nonzero exit; `"true"` always; `"false"` never. Booleans `true`/`false` are accepted too and are stored and returned as sent. A program that exits on its own has finished, however quickly it exits: any end under `"false"`, and an exit 0 under `"unexpected"`, is reported as `exited` as soon as it ends, with its exit code or its signal in `last_run`, and is held back until the startup window (`delay_seconds`; 1 second when 0) has passed, so a one-shot runs once; under `"true"` an exit 0 is held the same way and then started again. Under `"unexpected"` and `"true"` a non-zero exit or a signal inside that window is still a failed start, retried a limited number of times and then marked `fatal`. Hoody Kit programs keep the plain time-based rule: any exit before `delay_seconds` is a failed start, retried whatever this is.

directory.description: Working directory: an absolute path of ASCII letters and digits, `/`, `_`, `.`, `-`, space and tab, with no `..` path component, that must exist. Defaults to the user's home directory, or `/tmp`.

priority.description: Start priority, lower starts first. Defaults to 999. Any `u32` is accepted: nothing validates a range, so the value you send is the value stored and applied.

stdout_logfile.description: Path for standard output log. Must be under `/hoody/storage/hoody-daemon/logs`; any other path is a 400, because the log-reading endpoint refuses to read outside that root. Omitted, it defaults to `/hoody/storage/hoody-daemon/logs/<name>/stdout.log`.

stderr_logfile.description: Path for standard error log. Must be under `/hoody/storage/hoody-daemon/logs`; any other path is a 400, because the log-reading endpoint refuses to read outside that root. Omitted, it defaults to `/hoody/storage/hoody-daemon/logs/<name>/stderr.log`.

logs_enabled.description: Whether logging is enabled for this program. Default: true.

log_max_bytes.description: Maximum size of each log file in bytes before rotation. Default: 5242880 (5MB).

log_backups.description: Number of rotated backup log files to keep. Default: 2.

environment.description: Environment variables as key-value pairs. Names match `^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$` (up to 128 characters); values must not contain a line feed or carriage return, nor whitespace followed by `;` or `#` (the rest of the value would be read as a comment and the program could not load; refused with 400 unless the program has a `terminal_id` and no `port_range`; judged after line feeds, carriage returns and NULs are stripped). Nor may a value hold both a double and a single quote, or begin or end with either: values are written quoted with no escape character, so the first has no delimiter and the second arrives with the quote stripped (refused with 400 naming the variable, unless the program has a `terminal_id`, no `port_range` and a `user` other than root, for which such values are passed another way). A value with a double quote and no single quote is written in single quotes, any other in double quotes. The stored map is not the whole process environment: with `inject_computer_env` the program also receives PID 1's environment (Kit programs only its `HOODY_*` variables in the default mode), depending on the daemon's injection mode and on that environment being readable; without it, only the variables its `command` names. Explicit values override injected ones.

hoody_kit.description: Read-only. Server-derived: true when the program's directory is under `/hoody/plugins`, or when its name is a known Hoody Kit name AND its command is that kit program's. Any value supplied in a create or update request body is ignored.

inject_computer_env.description: Whether the daemon adds the computer's environment (PID 1's) to the program's. When absent: true for a Hoody Kit program (see `hoody_kit`), false for every other program. When true, the daemon's injection mode applies: by default a Kit program gets only the `HOODY_*` variables and any other program all of them; `--inject-all-env` and `--inject-hoody-env-only` override that for every program. When false, nothing from PID 1 is added, `HOODY_*` included, except the variables the program's `command` names as `$X`, `${X}` or `%(ENV_X)s`: each of those is resolved from the program's `environment`, then PID 1, then (for `$X` and `${X}` in a program without `port_range`) the daemon's own environment, and only that variable is added. A named variable is filtered like any other source: for a sandboxed program a value that is not literal, or a loader name, is dropped; a named variable with no value anywhere is left alone. This controls the daemon's own injection only: the program still inherits the environment of the process manager that runs it.

boot_if_exists.description: Absolute path of a marker file. Every time the daemon starts, it starts this program once if the path is a regular file (a symlink, a directory or a missing path does not count) and the process manager has not started the program since it came up. A program that is running stays as it is, and one that was stopped by hand stays stopped on a daemon restart or an update, but a reset stops and removes every program and replays the defaults, so after a reset a program whose file exists is started even if it had been stopped by hand; when the file is absent the program stays lazy. Meant for a lazy program (`lazy_load`) that must be running after a reboot only while it has work: the program keeps the file present while it does. The path must be absolute, contain no `..` segment and no control character, and be at most 4096 bytes. Allowed only for a standard program or a `port_range` of a single port (`start` equal to `end`); a wider range is refused with 400, on create and on an edit that widens the range of a program that has it. The daemon looks at the file only while it starts, never afterwards, so setting this field on an existing program starts nothing by itself. It does not change `boot` or `lazy_load`. An empty string is the same as leaving it out.

port_range.description: Port range for multi-instance programs. Each port in the range creates a separate INSTANCE (running process). Example: {start:8000, end:8099} creates 100 instances. Independent from lazy_load - can use with boot:true (all instances auto-start) OR lazy_load:true (instances start on-demand). A range must not overlap any other stored program's range. When either side has an effective sandbox, its ports are also compared with enabled programs' declared listening sets, and ports held by active or draining sandbox firewall records are refused until those records are gone. On edit the object replaces the stored range and needs both `start` and `end`.

end.description: Inclusive ending port, at least `start`. Both endpoints are 1 to 65535, and `end - start + 1` must not exceed 4096.

port_param.description: Parameter name for passing port (e.g. --port, -p). Valid ONLY together with port_range; sending it on its own is rejected with "port_param requires port_range to be set". Has no schema default on purpose. Omit it and the server applies --port itself, so a default here would make every port-less create fail.

lazy_load.description: Enable lazy loading. When true, program/instances NOT started automatically. Started on-demand by edge proxy via ensure-started endpoint. Cannot be combined with boot:true.

ready_port.description: TCP readiness port. When set, a start with `wait=true` is reported successful only once this port accepts a TCP connection, closing the gap where `running` only means "the startup window passed without an exit" while the listener is not up yet. The program must also be up: it is reported running, or it is still starting and only its own processes listen on this port, so a program that listens early is ready at once. For a program whose port lives inside its own command line rather than in a `port_range`. For a sandboxed program it joins `port_range` in the listening set that `sandbox.network.bind_ports` defaults to and must cover. The port counts as ready once the program accepts the TCP connection the daemon opens to it from inside the computer; a program that does not accept that connection never becomes ready (each attempt waits up to 300 ms). An accepted connection shows that something listens on that port, not that it is this program's listener or that it serves anything. `0` is refused. It is checked against active or draining sandbox firewall reservations, and against enabled programs' declared listening sets when either side has an effective sandbox; two unsandboxed programs' readiness ports are not compared. With `if_not_running`, an already-running or shared result can come back without this polling, and an already-running port-range instance is not probed.

stop_wait_seconds.description: Seconds a stop waits for the program to exit after the stop signal before it is killed, from 1 to 600. For a program that needs longer than the default 10 seconds to shut down cleanly. Omit it, or send 0, for the default.

display.description: Hoody Display number for GUI programs, 1 to 40000 (display 0 is not accepted; only screen 0, so ":1" or ":1.0"). Accepts "1", ":1" or the number 1. Before the program starts, the display is brought up (always in terminal N, where N is the display number, never in the program's own `terminal_id`) and the program's `user` is given access to it; if either fails, the request fails and the program is not started. For a persistent `boot` program the add, edit or enable is still saved in that case, but not applied. A display number equal to the program's own `terminal_id` is refused, and so are a display number equal to another program's `terminal_id` and a `terminal_id` equal to another program's display number, when the request creates that pairing. An edit that does not change `display` does not re-check a stored value.

terminal_id.description: Hoody Terminal integration: Session ID (1-65535). Designed for use with hoody-terminal web interface. When specified, program runs in that terminal: terminal N of the computer, opened at the `terminal-N` host in a browser, with `hoody daemon programs terminal connect`, or with the SDK's `client.daemon.programs.connectTerminal`. The program's input and output are connected to that terminal session. Must be unique among persistent programs. Cannot be combined with an effective `sandbox`, or with `port_range` (a port-range program has no terminal; a program stored with both is not refused an edit that leaves them). The program runs as its `user`, root or not, and gets `TERM=xterm-256color` unless its environment sets `TERM`. When the command ends, the program ends with the command's exit code, so its status and `autorestart` follow the command, and clients attached to its terminal are disconnected with WebSocket close code 4404 (`daemon program ended`); a restarted program is reached by attaching again. In interactive mode that is when the shell left after the command ends, and with `tmux` when the tmux client does. Output the program writes while hoody-terminal has no connection to it waits in the terminal, up to about 19 KB, and a program that writes more blocks until something attaches; once anything has attached or used the terminal's REST automation, hoody-terminal stays connected until the program ends or the terminal session is deleted. Output that reaches hoody-terminal, the program's stderr included, is also written to the program's stdout log as raw terminal output (control sequences and `\r\n` line ends kept), with the same size limit and rotation as any program's log, so its last output can still be read with the program's logs after it ends, when its terminal no longer answers. Two kinds of output are not in that log: output still waiting in the terminal when the program ends because nothing had attached, and output written faster than the log takes it in. The stderr log holds errors from setting up the terminal and from its connections; warnings are left out. A stop ends everything the program runs in its terminal: TERM first, KILL after 7 s for whatever ignores it.

terminal_shell.description: Hoody Terminal integration: the shell that loads the environment, or `tmux`. A non-blank value requires `terminal_id`, and the daemon accepts only an installed `bash`, `zsh`, `fish`, `sh` or `tmux`. A blank string means direct execution, like an omitted one. With a shell, the command is one shell command line (pipes, `&&` and variables work); without one, its words are passed as they are, with quotes grouping words and nothing expanded, and, as for a program without a terminal, a `#` or `;` after a space starts a comment, even inside quotes. Omit it, or send null, for direct execution.

terminal_interactive.description: Hoody Terminal integration: Override auto-detection of interactive vs service mode. true = interactive (-ic, shell persists), false = service (-c, exec replaces shell), undefined = auto-detect (recommended). Works with hoody-terminal web interface. In service mode the shell loads its rc file and is replaced by the command when it is a single command; a list, pipe or leading assignment runs as written. In interactive mode the command runs and the shell stays.

webhooks.description: Webhook notification configuration for program lifecycle events `enabled` and `urls` are REQUIRED whenever this object is present: the daemon's `WebhookConfig` has no default for either, so a webhooks object without them is a 400 from the add or edit handler (`invalid program body: missing field ...`). On an edit the two are replaced rather than merged, and only `events`, `headers`, `timeout` and `retry` keep their stored value when omitted, so a partial webhook edit has to resend `enabled` and `urls`. `webhooks: null` does not clear stored webhooks. Delivery needs more than this object: the daemon's `notifications.enabled` and `notifications.event_listener_enabled` must be true and the daemon's event listener must be running. Known limitation: event-driven delivery is not verified end to end; poll status for monitoring that has to be reliable.

enabled.description: Enable webhooks for this program

urls.description: Webhook URLs. When `enabled` is true: 1 to 5 URLs, HTTPS, no credentials, and public destinations only. A disabled configuration skips these checks. A name that resolves to a non-public address can save and then fail at delivery.

events.description: A single event name or an array, trimmed and case-insensitive: `STARTING`, `RUNNING`, `BACKOFF`, `STOPPING`, `STOPPED`, `EXITED`, `FATAL`, `UNKNOWN` (without `PROCESS_STATE_`). `[]`, `"all"` or `"*"` select all, and a new configuration without `events` selects all. On edit, omitted `events` keep the stored filter.

headers.description: Custom HTTP headers, at most 10 when `enabled` is true. On edit, supplied headers replace the stored map and omitted headers keep it.

timeout.description: Request timeout in seconds. When `enabled` is true it must be 1 to 60; when no value is stored the dispatcher uses 10.

retry.description: Retry attempts on failure. When `enabled` is true it must be 0 to 5; when no value is stored the dispatcher uses 3.

sandbox.description: Per-program confinement. Three-state on `programs/edit/{id}`: absent leaves the current block unchanged, `null` clears it, and an object REPLACES it as a unit. There is no field-level merge into a sandbox block, so an edit must resend every field it wants kept. On `programs/add` absent and `null` are the same thing. A policy rejection by the daemon's validation is a 400 carrying the usual `{success: false, error: ...}` envelope; a body that is not valid JSON, an unknown key inside `sandbox`, or a field of the wrong type is a 400 carrying the same envelope (`invalid program body: ...`). An accepted edit that changes the resolved policy replaces the loaded definition, which stops the instance running under the old one (whether a new one starts follows `boot` and `lazy_load`); an apply that fails after persistence is a 400 that says so, with the program persisted.

daemon_SandboxConfig.description:
Per-program filesystem, network and process confinement.

**When it applies.** The block is normalized first: defaults are filled, no-ops are dropped, and the block is EFFECTIVE only if a restriction remains (`read_only_root`, a non-empty `hidden`, `mode` other than `full`, a non-empty `ingress_allow_from`, `ingress_rate_limit`, `udp: deny` (in every mode, `none` included), `max_memory`, `max_pids`, `max_open_files`, `max_cpu`, `max_file_size`, `tmp_size` or `private_tmp`). A block that restricts nothing is stored as absent and the program runs exactly as it would without one.

**What changes for an effective block.** The program runs inside the sandbox: every Linux capability is dropped, it cannot gain privileges, and it cannot signal the computer's other processes or share their IPC. It can still see them: the process list stays visible. Consequences that callers must expect: the reported pid belongs to the sandbox around the program, not to the program itself; a signal death is reported as exit code `128+n` rather than as a signal; and any edit that changes the RESOLVED policy replaces the loaded definition, stopping the instance that ran under the old one, because the policy revision is part of the program's definition; whether a new instance starts follows `boot` and `lazy_load` (an edit that resolves to the same policy keeps the revision and is byte-idempotent: merged port ranges compare equal, while `writable`, `hidden` and `ingress_allow_from` keep their submitted order; a disabled program is removed instead; a lazy or non-boot program is installed without being started, so the edit does not by itself start an instance).

**Refusals.** `user` must resolve to a non-root account: an effective block on a `user: root` program is rejected with 400, because root inside the sandbox would still be root to the computer's system services and to the daemon's own process control. an effective block combined with `terminal_id` is a 400, and `quick-start` rejects any non-null `sandbox` value (`null` is absent). A stored block is validated whenever the program is rendered, not only when it restricts something, so a block that breaks a rule refuses the render instead of running the program unconfined. Every sub-object rejects unknown keys, so a misspelt field is a 400 rather than a silently weaker policy, which also means a field added by a newer client is a 400 against an older daemon. Every field of this object accepts an explicit `null`, which is treated exactly as if the field had been omitted. The object itself accepts `null` too: on add it is the same as no block; on EDIT a `null` `sandbox` CLEARS the stored block, while omitting the key preserves it (`sandbox` is the one field of an edit with that distinction).

daemon_SandboxFilesystem.description: Filesystem confinement. The program gets its own view of the filesystem, different from the rest of the computer's. Independently of these fields, every sandboxed program sees an empty `/run/user` in place of the real one, so it cannot reach its account's per-user service manager or session bus; a sandboxed program whose `directory` is under `/run/user` is rejected with 400. Unknown keys are rejected with 400. Every field of this object, and the object itself, accepts an explicit `null`, which is treated exactly as if the field had been omitted (only the top-level `sandbox` key of an edit distinguishes `null` from omission).

read_only_root.description: Make the whole filesystem read-only for the program. Every path outside `writable` answers EROFS, except `/dev`, the process information directory, a private `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`, and the mounts that hide `hidden` paths; ordinary account permissions still apply. `/sys` is read-only for every sandboxed program regardless of this flag, so the program cannot raise its own resource limits.

writable.description: Absolute directories the program may write to inside the read-only root. Each must already exist and is canonicalized. `read_only_root` must be true: `writable` on its own is a 400, not a restriction. A path may neither equal, contain, nor be contained by a protected root: the daemon's storage and configuration trees, the log base directory, `/etc`, `/run`, `/var/run`, `/hoody/plugins`, the process information directory, `/sys`, `/dev`, `/boot`, and the daemon executable's directory. `/hoody` and `/hoody/storage` are therefore refused because they contain the daemon's own tree; `/hoody/storage/apps/<name>` is accepted. At launch each path is canonicalized and its identity (device and inode) recorded, then checked again immediately before the sandbox starts; a path that changed identity, or is no longer a directory, is refused, and what is mounted writable is that approved directory itself. The comparison is between those two launch-time observations, not against the identity the API saw when the policy was stored. Where the directory appears is still resolved by pathname, so an actor who controls the path or a mutable ancestor can move where the approved object appears, never what it is. Needs a sandbox runtime that can mount a directory it already holds open (0.12.0 measured).

hidden.description: Absolute directories replaced by an empty, unreadable tmpfs (`--perms 0000 --tmpfs p`). Same both-direction overlap rule as `writable`, and additionally may not overlap `/usr`, `/bin`, `/sbin`, `/lib*`, `/hoody`, `/hoody/storage`, the program's own `directory`, or any `writable` entry.

daemon_SandboxNetwork.description: Network confinement. Outbound and bind restrictions (TCP, and `udp`) apply to each process of the program; inbound restrictions are applied by the computer's firewall to the program's listening ports. Unknown keys are rejected with 400. Every field of this object, and the object itself, accepts an explicit `null`, which is treated exactly as if the field had been omitted (only the top-level `sandbox` key of an edit distinguishes `null` from omission).

mode.description: `full` (default): no restriction on binding or connecting. Ingress settings still apply, so a `full` program can still carry an allowlist and a rate limit. `restricted`: TCP bind and connect are confined to `bind_ports` and `connect_ports` (needs `landlock_abi` 4 or higher in `/health`). The restriction is TCP-only, so UDP, ICMP and raw sockets are unaffected by this mode (`udp: deny` refuses UDP in every mode). So that the port lists hold, a `restricted` program also cannot create MPTCP or SMC sockets, cannot use io_uring and cannot send with `MSG_FASTOPEN`: an MPTCP request answers `EPROTONOSUPPORT`, `io_uring_setup` answers `ENOSYS` and a Fast Open send answers `EOPNOTSUPP`, so software that falls back to plain TCP, to epoll or to connect-then-send keeps working, and a program that requires io_uring does not run in this mode. `none`: the program gets no network at all (no interfaces), which closes IP and abstract unix sockets but NOT a unix socket reachable by filesystem path; `port_range`, `ready_port`, any non-null `bind_ports` (an empty list included), a non-empty `connect_ports` or `ingress_allow_from`, and any `ingress_rate_limit` are then rejected with 400; empty `connect_ports` / `ingress_allow_from` lists and `ingress_allow_platform` are accepted and inert.

bind_ports.description: TCP ports the program may bind (connecting is governed separately by `connect_ports`, and neither covers a socket that begins listening without binding). Overlapping and adjacent items are merged into disjoint ranges. Defaults to the union of `port_range` and `ready_port` (whichever are set), else empty; it is required for `mode: restricted` when neither is set, and must cover `port_range` and `ready_port` when those are set. This is also the listening set used for ingress rules and for port ownership, for an EFFECTIVE block only (a block that restricts nothing claims no ports): a port is reserved computer-wide across every local address, so a create or edit whose listening set overlaps another program's declared ports, a still-draining policy, the Hoody Kit ports or the daemon's own effective port is rejected with 400. Other programs' declared ports and installed firewall records are checked whenever a sandbox is involved on either side; two programs without a sandbox block keep the pre-sandbox rule (overlapping `port_range` values are refused, `ready_port` is not checked). Enabling a program re-checks ownership on the view it will have once enabled, whether or not it carries a sandbox block, so a program disabled while a sandboxed neighbour took its port is refused rather than brought back onto it. The Hoody Kit and daemon ports are reserved against sandboxed listening sets. Ports that an unsandboxed command opens without declaring them are unknowable and are not protected.

items.description: A single TCP port, or an inclusive range written "a-b".

connect_ports.description: TCP ports the program may connect to. Same item grammar as `bind_ports`. Valid only with `mode: restricted`; a non-empty list with any other mode is a 400.

items.description: A single TCP port, or an inclusive range written "a-b".

ingress_allow_from.description: Source networks allowed to open NEW connections to the listening set from outside the computer. Enforcement covers IPv4 TCP arriving on the computer's network interface. Rules match by destination PORT only, never by destination address. Established and related connections return before the allowlist is consulted, so tightening this field filters new connections and never cuts live ones. Because matching is per port, an undeclared service listening on the same port on another local address is filtered too. Requires a non-empty listening set. Maximum 64 entries, each a strict dotted-quad `a.b.c.d/n`.

ingress_allow_platform.description: Accept new connections whose source address is the computer itself or the computer's network gateway before the rate limit and the allowlist are consulted, so those sources are neither filtered nor throttled. The exemption matches the packet's source address, not the caller's identity. edge proxy forwards public traffic with the client's own address as the source, so that traffic meets the allowlist and the rate limit like any other source. A request a computer sends to a public service URL on its own server is not exempt either: it arrives from the server's public address. Default true. On its own it restricts nothing: a sandbox block whose only content is `ingress_allow_platform` normalizes to no sandbox at all and the program runs exactly as it would without one.

ingress_rate_limit.description: Per-source-address budget for new connections, `"N/s"` or `"N/m"` with N between 1 and 100000. Each source is tracked for 60 s, up to 65535 sources per policy; the budget is checked after the platform exception and BEFORE the allowlist; a policy with only a rate limit has no terminal drop, so sources within budget pass. Only new connections are metered, ECN-capable connection attempts included. Two documented consequences: budgets reset whenever the computer's sandbox firewall rules are reloaded: when any sandboxed program's inbound rules are added, changed or removed, and at every daemon start and reset; and once 65535 sources are tracked new sources are untracked, so the rate limit fails open while the allowlist keeps applying.

udp.description: `allow` (default): UDP is not restricted. `deny`: the program and everything it starts cannot create an IPv4 or IPv6 datagram socket (UDP, UDP-Lite and ICMP ping sockets all answer `EACCES`), nor an IPv4 or IPv6 SCTP socket of any type, including the one an IPv4 or IPv6 `SOCK_SEQPACKET` socket with protocol 0 selects (SCTP can carry itself in UDP) nor an `AF_RXRPC` socket (its transport is UDP), both `EACCES`, and cannot use io_uring (`io_uring_setup` answers `ENOSYS`, because a ring could create the socket without the system call). Raw sockets already need a capability no sandboxed program has. TCP and unix sockets are unaffected, and under `mode: restricted` every answer the restricted rules give is unchanged. Enforced inside the sandbox; a socket handed in by a process outside the sandbox (inherited, or passed over a unix socket) is not covered. A 32-bit (i386) program that creates sockets through `socketcall` cannot create any socket under `deny`, TCP and unix included, because that call's arguments cannot be inspected; the direct 32-bit `socket` call gets the selective rule. **Name resolution:** glibc asks its name servers over UDP first and does not fall back to TCP when the socket is refused, so the program reads a per-launch copy of the computer's `/etc/resolv.conf` with `options use-vc` added, which makes glibc ask over TCP; the copy is bound over the file `/etc/resolv.conf` resolves to as the last mount and removed when the launch ends. The launch is refused when `/etc/resolv.conf` is missing, not a regular file or larger than 64 KiB, or when it resolves through a private tmp, a `writable` path, a `hidden` path or a masked directory (`/run/user`, `/dev`). Under `mode: restricted` the name servers' TCP port 53 must be in `connect_ports`; it is not added for you. musl and resolvers that ignore `resolv.conf` options need their own TCP DNS configuration. Under `mode: none` the field is kept and still applies (a program with no network can still create a UDP socket); no resolver copy is made, since there is no name server to reach.

daemon_SandboxProcess.description: Process limits, applied three ways: `max_memory`, `max_pids` and `max_cpu` to the program and everything it starts, taken together (each is read back before the program runs; a limit that did not land refuses the launch); `max_open_files` and `max_file_size` per process, set just before the program starts; and `private_tmp` and `tmp_size` as the program's own temporary directories. The program sees `/sys` read-only and cannot raise these limits. Unknown keys are rejected with 400. Every field of this object, and the object itself, accepts an explicit `null`, which is treated exactly as if the field had been omitted (only the top-level `sandbox` key of an edit distinguishes `null` from omission).

max_memory.description: Memory ceiling, from 16M to 64G, written as `<n>[KMG]` in binary units or as a plain decimal byte count in the same range. A bare decimal is a byte count (`"536870912"` and `"512M"` are the same limit). It covers the program and everything it starts, and swap is not allowed, so the limit cannot be passed by swapping. When it is hit, the kernel kills one of the program's processes to free memory, which is not necessarily the one that asked for more, and the others keep running; when the process killed is the program itself it exits with 137 and the rest of its processes are then stopped.

max_pids.description: Maximum number of processes and threads, from 4 to 65536. The sandbox itself uses 2 of them, so budget at least 2 above the program's own process and thread count.

max_open_files.description: `RLIMIT_NOFILE`, soft and hard, from 8 to 1048576. Set last, inside the sandbox, immediately before the program is exec'd, so the files the sandbox itself holds open are not charged against it.

max_cpu.description: CPU ceiling for the program and everything it starts, `"<n>%"` with n from 1 to 102400, where 100% is one CPU's worth (`"250%"` is two and a half CPUs). Before the program runs, the applied ceiling is read back and the launch is refused if there is none or it is more than 1 % away from the request. It is a ceiling on the whole process tree, not a reservation. Per instance: a `port_range` program with N instances has N separate ceilings, so the instances together may use N × n%.

max_file_size.description: Largest size any single regular file the program writes may reach, from 1K to 1024G, in the size grammar of `max_memory` (`<n>[KMG]` in binary units or a plain byte count; there is no `T`, so a terabyte is `1024G`). Set as `RLIMIT_FSIZE`, soft and hard, immediately before the program is exec'd. A write past the limit fails with `EFBIG`. The kernel also sends `SIGXFSZ`, but programs started by the daemon inherit that signal ignored, so the usual outcome is a write error the program handles rather than a kill. It is not a disk quota: it bounds each file's growth, not the total written, and the program's output logs are not covered.

tmp_size.description: Size of EACH of the program's private `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`, from 1M to 64G, in the size grammar of `max_memory`. Requires `private_tmp: true`; on its own it is a 400. Applies to the two private directories only, so the two together may hold up to twice this value; a write past it fails with `ENOSPC`. Their contents are held in memory, so they also count against `max_memory`. Needs sandbox runtime support (`/health` reports `bwrap_tmpfs_size`); without it the launch is refused.

private_tmp.description: Give the program its own empty `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`, invisible to the rest of the computer. Rejected with 400 when a `filesystem.writable` entry equals, contains or is contained by `/tmp` or `/var/tmp`: the private mounts are applied first, so a writable bind over them would expose the computer's shared directory. Also rejected when the program's `directory` lies strictly below `/tmp` or `/var/tmp`, or when the daemon itself is installed below either: the private mounts would hide them and the launch could not reach the program. Without `tmp_size` the two mounts take the kernel's tmpfs default size (half of RAM each).

daemon_ProgramInstance.description: Represents a running instance of a port-range program. Each instance is an actual process running on a specific port.

port.description: Port number this instance is running on

status.description: Current runtime status of this instance. Lowercased process state name; `stopped` is returned when the daemon cannot query program states at all; `unknown` when the query gets no answer or an unreadable one. `exited` is also the status of a run that has ended while the daemon is still finishing up after it; `supervisor_state` then carries the underlying process state.

pid.description: Process ID when running; omitted otherwise

uptime.description: Uptime as "H:MM:SS", or "N day(s), H:MM:SS" once the process has been up for more than a day. Omitted when not running.

supervisor_state.description: The underlying process state, present only when it differs from `status`: a program whose run has ended while the daemon is still finishing up after it is `exited` in `status` while this says `running` (or `starting`).

last_run.description: The last ended run. Absent before the first run ends.

stats.description: Resource stats for this instance's process tree. Only present when include_stats=true and the instance is running.

daemon_ProgramStatus.description: Runtime status for a standard (non-port-range) program

status.description: Current runtime status of the program. Lowercased process state name; `stopped` is returned when the daemon cannot query program states at all; `unknown` when the query gets no answer or an unreadable one. `exited` is also the status of a run that has ended while the daemon is still finishing up after it; `supervisor_state` then carries the underlying process state. `partial` is only ever the status `GET /status` lists for a port-range program: some of its instances are starting or running and some are not.

pid.description: Process ID when running; omitted otherwise

uptime.description: Uptime as "H:MM:SS", or "N day(s), H:MM:SS" once the process has been up for more than a day. Omitted when the program is not running. No `pattern` is declared: the day form varies (`1 day,` / `2 days,`) and pinning a regex here would make valid responses invalid.

supervisor_state.description: The underlying process state, present only when it differs from `status`: a program whose run has ended while the daemon is still finishing up after it is `exited` in `status` while this says `running` (or `starting`).

last_run.description: The last ended run. Absent before the first run ends.

code.description: Machine-readable error code, present on some errors. `INVALID_QUERY`: a list route was given a query parameter it does not accept.

example.error: User "invalid-user" does not exist on the system

id.description: Not sent by this endpoint. `id` is omitted from the add response (the field is skipped when absent), so read the new id from `program.id`. It is carried by the responses that have no `program` to put it in, such as remove.

daemon_StatusResponse.description: Runtime status for one program. Three shapes are returned, distinguished by which field is present: standard programs carry `status`; a port-range program queried with a `port` carries `instance`; a port-range program queried without one carries `instances` plus `running_count`/`total_count`/`summary`. Only `success` is common to all three, which is why it is the sole required field.

stats.description: Standard (non-port-range) programs only: resource stats for the program's process tree. Port-range programs carry their stats on each instance instead (ProgramInstance.stats), whether one port was asked about or all of them. Only present when include_stats=true and the program is running.

instance.description: Port-range programs, single-port query: the one instance that was asked about.

instances.description: Port-range programs, no port given: one entry per non-stopped instance.

running_count.description: Port-range programs: number of instances that are `starting` or `running`. `instances` lists every non-stopped instance, so it can be longer: check each instance's own `status`.

total_count.description: Port-range programs: total number of possible instances (0 for a stored range whose end is lower than its start)

summary.description: Port-range programs, no port given: one status for the range, from the instances in `instances`. The state they all share; `running` when every one is starting or running; `partial` when some are and some are not; `stopped` when none is listed, or none is up and their states differ.

daemon_SandboxStatus.description: What the daemon would enforce for one program (`effective`) beside what the kernel is actually holding (`live`). Diagnostic only. Nothing here is settable.

configured.description: The stored sandbox block, exactly as persisted, or null when the program has none. A stored block can still be non-effective only if the saved program list was edited by hand; the API stores a block that restricts nothing as absent.

rev.description: Policy revision: the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the canonical spec. It is part of the program's installed definition and of the rule set name in `live.chain`; each launch's name in `scope_argv` carries the first six of those digits. A policy change is a new identity rather than an edit of the old one. Null when the program has no effective sandbox, and also when its stored policy no longer validates (then `problems` says why).

effective.description: The argument vectors the daemon builds from the stored policy. This is what the policy resolves to, not a reading of a running process. Null whenever `rev` is null.

bwrap_argv.description: The command line that applies the filesystem and isolation part of the policy: isolation flags, the root mount, the `writable` and `hidden` mounts, and the working directory. Each launch opens every writable directory itself and hands it to the sandbox, shown here as `<opened-at-launch>`, so the rendering is diagnostic and not runnable as printed. Its exact contents can change between daemon versions; do not parse it.

scope_argv.description: The command line that applies the process limits (`max_memory`, `max_pids`, `max_cpu`). Each launch gets its own name, which carries the program id and the first six digits of `rev`. Its exact contents can change between daemon versions; do not parse it.

live.description: `table_present` and `rules` are read from the kernel at request time; `chain` is the name this program's current revision owns, derived from the stored policy. `table_present: false` also covers a table that could not be read.

table_present.description: Whether the `ip hoody_daemon` table exists. It is absent when the committed state holds no active and no draining record. The daemon never leaves an empty table behind. A record still draining for a removed or edited program keeps the table until its instances have stopped, so "no program has an ingress policy" does not by itself mean "no table".

chain.description: The name of the inbound rule set this program's current revision owns when the policy has ingress rules; null for a policy with only filesystem and process limits. The name follows from the stored revision, so it can name a rule set that is not installed (`rules` is then empty); it is null when the installed rules could not be read at all. During a drain the previous revision's rule set also exists under its own name; on ports the two policies share, a packet must pass both allowlists.

rules.description: The chain's rules in the firewall's JSON format, objects of the form `{"rule": {...}}`, in evaluation order. Empty when the chain does not exist or the table could not be read.

firewall.description: `ok`: this program's current revision holds an active record and the installed rules match what the last successful apply recorded. `degraded`: the obligation could not be verified; every reason is a line in `problems` (sandbox firewall rules that are missing, unreadable or changed outside the daemon, a policy that no longer validates, sandbox state that cannot be read, an enabled program's policy owing rules without a record (a disabled program owes none: its record is admitted when it is enabled), or an earlier definition of this program that may still be running unconfined). The sources `ingress_rate_limit` is tracking are not compared, so they never cause this. `degraded` takes precedence over `draining`. `draining`: a previous revision of this program's policy (even one whose block has since been cleared) is still installed under its own rule set because instances running under it have not been confirmed stopped; both revisions' rules apply until they are, and the old listening set stays reserved. `none` (verified): this program holds no active or draining record under any revision and owes no rules; other programs' rules may still be installed. An active record left by another revision of this program is reported as a problem instead.

problems.description: Why `firewall` is `degraded`, one line per reason: the live table is missing, unreadable, or does not match the committed fingerprint; the stored policy no longer validates (its ports taken, a path gone); the saved firewall state cannot be read; the policy of an ENABLED program owes ingress rules and holds no active or draining record (a disabled program is admitted when it is enabled, so it owes none); or an earlier definition of this program may still be running without the confinement its policy declares, in which case its records are retained and its listening set stays reserved. That last one appears only while the program still owns an active or draining record, because there are otherwise no rules to retain, and it lists the program groups that have to be checked. Four things clear it: an apply that was confirmed taken up, a confirmed removal of the program's installed definition, a later quarantine of the same program whose own check finds nothing running or finds it running confined, and a check at the next daemon start. A still-failing apply can therefore release the reservation, and a hold whose group names could not be determined at all is kept until an apply or a removal of the program succeeds, because there is nothing to check. Empty exactly when `firewall` is not `degraded`. The endpoint answers 200 for every existing program; only an unknown id is 404.

daemon_EphemeralProgram.description: Ephemeral (temporary) program. Not saved with the permanent programs; tracked separately. Its definition is withdrawn once it finishes, is stopped or expires; its entry (status, `last_run`) stays readable for 10 minutes after that, and its log files are never deleted.

temporary_id.description: Unique temporary identifier, `quick_<unix-ms>_<sequence>`. The sequence is a process-wide counter that keeps two launches in the same millisecond apart.

command.description: Command to execute. Must not contain a line feed, carriage return or NUL.

user.description: System user to run as. A Linux account name matched case-insensitively: starts with a letter or `_`, continues with letters, digits, `_` and `-`, may end in `$`, at most 32 bytes. Quick-start programs cannot be sandboxed.

display.description: X11 DISPLAY number (normalized with ":" prefix)

status.description: Current runtime status

pid.description: Process ID when running

uptime.description: Uptime, `H:MM:SS` or with a day prefix such as `1 day, 2:03:04`.

created_at.description: ISO timestamp when program was created

expires_at.description: The absolute execution deadline: the launch time plus `ttl`. Absent without a TTL.

supervisor_state.description: The underlying process state, present only when it differs from `status`: a program whose run has ended while the daemon is still finishing up after it is `exited` in `status` while this says `running` (or `starting`).

last_run.description: The program's last ended run, once it has one.

daemon_EphemeralProgramInput.description: Input for creating ephemeral (temporary) program via quick-start

command.description: Command to execute with full arguments for your custom program/script. Custom code only; system services (`apache2`, `nginx`, etc.) belong under `systemctl`. Must not contain a line feed, carriage return or NUL.

user.description: System user to run as (must exist on the system). A Linux account name matched case-insensitively: starts with a letter or `_`, continues with letters, digits, `_` and `-`, may end in `$`, at most 32 bytes. Quick-start programs cannot be sandboxed.

name.description: Custom name (auto-generated if omitted). Starts with a letter or digit and contains only letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_`, up to 128 characters.

autorestart.description: Restart policy: `"false"` (default for a quick-start) never restarts; `"unexpected"` restarts after an exit code other than 0, including a deliberate nonzero exit; `"true"` always. Booleans `true`/`false` are accepted too and are stored and returned as sent. Omitted, a quick-start runs once: any end, whatever its exit code or signal, is reported as `exited` with the code or signal in `last_run` (with `wait: true`, a 200), and a command that cannot be executed fails once and is not retried. A quick-start that should be restarted after a crash, such as a temporary server, sets `"unexpected"` or `"true"`. Persistent programs keep `"unexpected"` as their default. A program that exits on its own has finished, however quickly it exits: any end under `"false"`, and an exit 0 under `"unexpected"`, is reported as `exited` as soon as it ends, with its exit code or its signal in `last_run`, and is held back until the startup window (`delay_seconds`; 1 second when 0) has passed, so a one-shot runs once; under `"true"` an exit 0 is held the same way and then started again. Under `"unexpected"` and `"true"` a non-zero exit or a signal inside that window is still a failed start, retried a limited number of times and then marked `fatal`.

directory.description: Working directory: an absolute path of ASCII letters and digits, `/`, `_`, `.`, `-`, space and tab, with no `..` path component, that must exist. Defaults to the user's home directory, or `/tmp`.

environment.description: Environment variables as key-value pairs. Names match `^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$` (up to 128 characters); values must not contain a line feed or carriage return, nor whitespace followed by `;` or `#` (the rest of the value would be read as a comment and the program could not load; refused with 400 unless the program has a `terminal_id` and no `port_range`; judged after line feeds, carriage returns and NULs are stripped). Nor may a value hold both a double and a single quote, or begin or end with either: values are written quoted with no escape character, so the first has no delimiter and the second arrives with the quote stripped (refused with 400 naming the variable, unless the program has a `terminal_id`, no `port_range` and a `user` other than root, for which such values are passed another way). A value with a double quote and no single quote is written in single quotes, any other in double quotes. The stored map is not the whole process environment: with `inject_computer_env: true` the program also receives PID 1's environment, depending on the daemon's injection mode and on that environment being readable; without it, only the variables its `command` names. Explicit values override injected ones.

inject_computer_env.description: Whether the daemon adds the computer's environment (PID 1's) to the program's. Absent means false for a quick-start, whatever its directory. When true, the daemon's injection mode applies (all variables by default; `--inject-hoody-env-only` limits it to `HOODY_*`). When false, nothing from PID 1 is added except the variables the `command` names as `$X`, `${X}` or `%(ENV_X)s`, resolved from `environment`, then PID 1, then (for `$X` and `${X}`) the daemon's own environment. The program still inherits the environment of the process manager that runs it.

priority.description: Start priority, lower starts first. Defaults to 999. No range is enforced here either.

delay_seconds.description: The startup window: seconds the program must STAY RUNNING for the start to count as successful. Nothing is postponed: the program is launched immediately. NOTE that 0 does NOT disable the window: at 0 the window is 1 second. Under `autorestart` `"unexpected"` or `"true"`, a non-zero exit or a signal inside the window is a FAILED start, retried a limited number of times and then marked `fatal`. An end that is not a crash under `autorestart` (any end under `"false"`, an exit 0 otherwise) is not a failed start, however quick: the daemon holds it back until the window has passed, so a one-shot runs once. Under `"false"` and `"unexpected"` it is reported as `exited` as soon as it ends, with its exit code or its signal in `last_run`; under `"true"` it is not reported as `exited` and is started again once the window has passed. A stop, edit or removal sent in that window can take up to this long to return.

stdout_logfile.description: Path for standard output log. Must be under `/hoody/storage/hoody-daemon/logs`; any other path is a 400, because the log-reading endpoint refuses to read outside that root. Omitted, it defaults to `/hoody/storage/hoody-daemon/logs/<name>/stdout.log`.

stderr_logfile.description: Path for standard error log. Must be under `/hoody/storage/hoody-daemon/logs`; any other path is a 400, because the log-reading endpoint refuses to read outside that root. Omitted, it defaults to `/hoody/storage/hoody-daemon/logs/<name>/stderr.log`.

logs_enabled.description: Whether logging is enabled for this program. Default: true.

log_max_bytes.description: Maximum size of each log file in bytes before rotation. Default: 5242880 (5MB).

log_backups.description: Number of rotated backup log files to keep. Default: 2.

ttl.description: Time-to-live in seconds, counted from launch (when the daemon dispatches the start) and bounding the whole execution, across retries and restarts (a 64-bit unsigned integer on the wire, 0 to 18446744073709551615; a JavaScript number is exact only up to 2^53 - 1). The deadline is returned as `expires_at`. Expiry is checked every 10 seconds, so it is not an exact deadline; `0` expires at the first check. The deadline arithmetic saturates, so a very large value means no practical expiry rather than an overflow.

wait.description: Wait for program to reach RUNNING state before returning

timeout.description: Seconds to wait for the program to be running when `wait=true` (default 30). The server clamps it to 300.

display.description: Hoody Display number for GUI programs, 1 to 40000 (display 0 is not accepted; only screen 0, so ":1" or ":1.0"). Accepts "1", ":1" or the number 1. Before the program starts, the display is brought up (always in terminal N, where N is the display number, never in the program's own `terminal_id`) and the program's `user` is given access to it; if either fails, the request fails and the program is not started. For a persistent `boot` program the add, edit or enable is still saved in that case, but not applied. A display number equal to the program's own `terminal_id` is refused. An edit that does not change `display` does not re-check a stored value.

terminal_id.description: Hoody Terminal integration: session id. Quick-start does not check it for uniqueness, and its wire type accepts 0 to 65535; choose an unused id. The program runs in terminal N of the computer, opened at the `terminal-N` host. The program runs as its `user`, root or not, and gets `TERM=xterm-256color` unless its environment sets `TERM`. When the command ends, the program ends with the command's exit code, so its status and `autorestart` follow the command, and clients attached to its terminal are disconnected with WebSocket close code 4404 (`daemon program ended`); a restarted program is reached by attaching again. In interactive mode that is when the shell left after the command ends, and with `tmux` when the tmux client does. Output the program writes while hoody-terminal has no connection to it waits in the terminal, up to about 19 KB, and a program that writes more blocks until something attaches; once anything has attached or used the terminal's REST automation, hoody-terminal stays connected until the program ends or the terminal session is deleted. Output that reaches hoody-terminal, the program's stderr included, is also written to the program's stdout log as raw terminal output (control sequences and `\r\n` line ends kept), with the same size limit and rotation as any program's log, so its last output can still be read with the program's logs after it ends, when its terminal no longer answers. Two kinds of output are not in that log: output still waiting in the terminal when the program ends because nothing had attached, and output written faster than the log takes it in. The stderr log holds errors from setting up the terminal and from its connections; warnings are left out. A stop ends everything the program runs in its terminal: TERM first, KILL after 7 s for whatever ignores it.

terminal_shell.description: Hoody Terminal integration: shell wrapper for environment loading. Quick-start does not validate the name or check that the shell is installed, and a shell without `terminal_id` is ignored. A blank string means direct execution.

terminal_interactive.description: Hoody Terminal integration: Override auto-detection. true=interactive (-ic), false=service (-c), undefined=auto-detect. For use with hoody-terminal. In service mode the shell loads its rc file and is replaced by the command when it is a single command; a list, pipe or leading assignment runs as written. In interactive mode the command runs and the shell stays.

daemon_QuickStartResponse.description: Response from the quick-start endpoints. A success carries `temporary_id`, `name`, `status` and `created_at`; an error carries `error`, and `temporary_id` whenever the program was created.

temporary_id.description: Unique temporary identifier for this ephemeral program

display.description: X11 DISPLAY number (normalized with ":" prefix)

status.description: Current program status. A finished program answers the status it finished with (`exited`, `fatal`, `stopped`, or `failed` when its definition never loaded) for 10 minutes after it finished.

pid.description: Process ID (if wait=true and running)

uptime.description: Uptime as "H:MM:SS", or "N day(s), H:MM:SS" once the process has been up for more than a day. Omitted when not running.

created_at.description: ISO timestamp when program was created

expires_at.description: The absolute execution deadline: the launch time plus `ttl`. A program still running then is stopped, and its `last_run.error` reads `ttl expired`. Absent without a TTL.

supervisor_state.description: The underlying process state, present only when it differs from `status`: a program whose run has ended while the daemon is still finishing up after it is `exited` in `status` while this says `running` (or `starting`).

last_run.description: The program's last ended run. Present once it has finished, and on a launch error that has a result.

error.description: Present when `success` is false. Every error after the program is created comes with its `temporary_id`.

count.description: Number of ephemeral programs currently tracked

cleaned_up.description: Whether the program's definition is withdrawn. `false` means the withdrawal is retried in the background; the result is recorded either way.

message.example: Program stopped; its result and logs stay readable for 10 minutes

example.message: Program stopped; its result and logs stay readable for 10 minutes

log_file.description: Path to the log file that was read

daemon_ProcessInfo.description: Resource stats for a single process in the process tree

pid.description: Process ID

command.description: Command line of the process

cpu_percent.description: CPU usage percentage (can exceed 100% on multi-core systems). This is a lifetime average (total CPU time divided by the process's age), not instantaneous usage.

daemon_ProgramStats.description: Aggregated resource stats for a program including its full process tree (root process + all child/descendant processes).

pid.description: Root process ID of the program's process tree

started_at.description: ISO 8601 timestamp of when the process started

cpu_percent.description: Total CPU usage percentage across all processes in the tree (can exceed 100% on multi-core). This is a lifetime average (total CPU time divided by the process's age), not instantaneous usage.

memory_rss_bytes.description: Total Resident Set Size in bytes across all processes in the tree

process_count.description: Number of processes in the tree (root + children)

processes.description: Per-process breakdown of the process tree

daemon_ProgramPortRangeStatus.description: Runtime status of a port-range program: aggregate counts plus one entry per non-stopped instance.

type.description: Discriminator. Present only on port-range status objects; standard programs carry `id`/`status` instead.

status.description: One status for the range, by the same rule as `summary` on `GET /status/{id}`: the state every listed instance shares, `running`, `partial` (some instances up and some not), `stopped`, or `unknown` when the instances could not be read.

states_known.description: `false` when the instances could not be read: `status` is then `unknown`, and `running_instances` and `instances` say nothing. Never read that as stopped.

running_instances.description: Number of instances that are `starting` or `running`; an instance whose run has ended is not counted, though it is listed.

total_instances.description: Total number of possible instances (port_range.end - port_range.start + 1; 0 for a stored range whose end is lower than its start)

daemon_ProgramUpdate.description: The fields to change on an existing program. Every one is optional and an omitted field keeps its stored value: this is a merge, not a replacement. `sandbox: null` clears the block, while a `sandbox` object replaces it whole. `id` is taken from the path and ignored in the body. Same validation as `ProgramInput` for every field that is present, including the port-ownership checks, which run against the program's view once the change is applied.

id.description: Ignored on edit: the path id identifies the program and is preserved.

name.description: Program name. Must be unique, start with a letter or digit, and contain only letters, digits, `.`, `-` and `_`, up to 128 characters.

command.description: Command to execute with full arguments for your custom program. Use only for custom applications/scripts; system services (`apache2`, `nginx`, `mysql`, etc.) belong under `systemctl`. Must not contain a line feed, carriage return or NUL.

user.description: System user (must exist on the system). A Linux account name matched case-insensitively: starts with a letter or `_`, continues with letters, digits, `_` and `-`, may end in `$`, at most 32 bytes. A sandboxed program cannot run as an account resolving to uid 0.

enabled.description: Enable the program immediately

boot.description: Start automatically on system boot. A program with a `display` is started as soon as that display is ready.

delay_seconds.description: The startup window: seconds the program must STAY RUNNING for the start to count as successful. Nothing is postponed: the program is launched immediately. NOTE that 0 does NOT disable the window: at 0 the window is 1 second. Under `autorestart` `"unexpected"` or `"true"`, a non-zero exit or a signal inside the window is a FAILED start, retried a limited number of times and then marked `fatal`. An end that is not a crash under `autorestart` (any end under `"false"`, an exit 0 otherwise) is not a failed start, however quick: the daemon holds it back until the window has passed, so a one-shot runs once. Under `"false"` and `"unexpected"` it is reported as `exited` as soon as it ends, with its exit code or its signal in `last_run`; under `"true"` it is not reported as `exited` and is started again once the window has passed. A stop, edit or removal sent in that window can take up to this long to return. Hoody Kit programs keep the plain rule: the window is also 1 second at 0, and any exit inside the window is a failed start, whatever `autorestart` says.

autorestart.description: Restart policy: `"unexpected"` restarts after an exit code other than 0, including a deliberate nonzero exit; `"true"` always; `"false"` never. Booleans `true`/`false` are accepted too and are stored and returned as sent. A program that exits on its own has finished, however quickly it exits: any end under `"false"`, and an exit 0 under `"unexpected"`, is reported as `exited` as soon as it ends, with its exit code or its signal in `last_run`, and is held back until the startup window (`delay_seconds`; 1 second when 0) has passed, so a one-shot runs once; under `"true"` an exit 0 is held the same way and then started again. Under `"unexpected"` and `"true"` a non-zero exit or a signal inside that window is still a failed start, retried a limited number of times and then marked `fatal`. Hoody Kit programs keep the plain time-based rule: any exit before `delay_seconds` is a failed start, retried whatever this is. Omitted or null on edit, the stored policy is kept; the create default is `"unexpected"`.

directory.description: Working directory: an absolute path of ASCII letters and digits, `/`, `_`, `.`, `-`, space and tab, with no `..` path component, that must exist. Omitted, the stored directory is kept, even when `user` changes.

priority.description: Start priority, lower starts first. Omitted, the stored value is kept. Any `u32` is accepted: nothing validates a range, so the value you send is the value stored and applied.

stdout_logfile.description: Path for standard output log. Must be under `/hoody/storage/hoody-daemon/logs`; any other path is a 400, because the log-reading endpoint refuses to read outside that root. Omitted or null, the stored path is kept.

stderr_logfile.description: Path for standard error log. Must be under `/hoody/storage/hoody-daemon/logs`; any other path is a 400, because the log-reading endpoint refuses to read outside that root. Omitted or null, the stored path is kept.

logs_enabled.description: Whether logging is enabled for this program. Omitted, the stored value is kept.

log_max_bytes.description: Maximum size of each log file in bytes before rotation. Omitted, the stored value is kept.

log_backups.description: Number of rotated backup log files to keep. Omitted, the stored value is kept.

environment.description: Environment variables as key-value pairs. Names match `^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$` (up to 128 characters); values must not contain a line feed or carriage return, nor whitespace followed by `;` or `#` (the rest of the value would be read as a comment and the program could not load; refused with 400 unless the program has a `terminal_id` and no `port_range`; judged after line feeds, carriage returns and NULs are stripped). Nor may a value hold both a double and a single quote, or begin or end with either: values are written quoted with no escape character, so the first has no delimiter and the second arrives with the quote stripped (refused with 400 naming the variable, unless the program has a `terminal_id`, no `port_range` and a `user` other than root, for which such values are passed another way).
